#10262. The Lenovo Legion Tab Gen 5 would be my perfect Steam tablet if it didn’t cost $900

For every Android-powered slate I’ve used, only Nvidia’s Shield Tablet really stands out in my memory. Part of the company’s occasional (and all-but-dead) dip into hardware products, the Shield Tablet — and its revitalized K1 follow-up, which I also owned through a recall program on the original — carried me through the back half of college, frequently keeping my Chromebook in my backpack in lieu of a mini Bluetooth keyboard or the Shield Tablet’s built-in stylus. Its front-firing speakers made it great for movie-watching, and while I’m not much of a mobile gamer, I did find it to be a great device for emulation, especially when paired with an external controller.

Even if Nvidia hadn’t abandoned the hardware game at the end of the last decade, it’s found new and much more destructive ways to make piles of cash at the expense of your easy access to RAM. And considering the market for Android tablets in general, it’s not all too surprising to see very few companies trying to make headway into offering a miniature, gaming-focused tablet that can easily be thrown in a backpack. Lenovo, however, has managed to fill its spot quite well. 9to5Google’s own Ben Schoon found himself smitten with the Gen 3 model nearly two years ago, and now, its Gen 5 successor has found its way into my nostalgic hands.

But expectations around mobile experiences have come a long way since 2016. Whether the Legion Tab Gen 5 can win over your heart really depends on your patience with some old-school Android jank — and whether your wallet can withstand an exceptionally-high asking price. Still, with recent advancements in PC emulation, it’s hard to say Lenovo isn’t onto something.

Considering the decade between their respective releases, I’m actually quite surprised just how much this tablet reminds me of the original Shield Tablet. Its 8.8-inch 16:10 LCD panel combined with a boxy matte-black design and a near-identical weight meant that I immediately felt at home holding this thing in my hands. You lose out on a couple of clutch features — most notably the built-in stylus — but largely speaking, this feels like the correct size and shape for a miniature gaming tablet.

Still, it’s not all perfect. Take, for example, the completely unnecessary camera bump that prevents this slate from properly laying flat on a desk. No one is buying this thing to use the camera, and judging by my very limited experience trying it out, I’m fairly confident whatever potato sensor is shoved in here would fit fine flush with the chassis. I’m pretty fed up with OEMs leaning on camera bumps to make any device look or feel more premium than it actually is, and that goes double quadruple for tablets like this.

Just like its predecessor, this thing still picks up smudges and fingerprints at an unreasonable level, its matte-black finish unable to hide anything. 360 grams is also a little heavier than I’d expect for a slate of this size, though to be fair, it’s much more noticeable in portrait than landscape. Holding the tablet with two hands to watch a movie or make my way through another round of Balatro made its top-heaviness much less noticeable.

This display is sharp and fast — with one minor caveat — and reasonably bright in all circumstances except direct sunlight thanks to its 600 nits of brightness (and 800 in HBM). Really, it’s the LCD of it all that gets me here; this thing is nearly $1,000, and the lack of OLED alone makes it difficult to recommend at this price. It’s not an outright bad panel, but I found its contrast levels to be pretty lacking, with most blacks only ever showing up as dark grays on-screen.

Oh, and that caveat: On two different occasions, I caught the tablet stuck in 60Hz mode, regardless of what refresh rate option I selected in settings. Switching back and forth between modes a few times eventually unstuck it, but it’s definitely a bug worth being aware of.

I think I’d feel a lot better about recommending this to someone looking for a content consumption device if this screen looked a little more premium. Your mileage may vary though — if you can get your hands on a demo unit before buying one, if only to see the display, I’d recommend it. For everyone else, this price tag might have you waiting for the OLED panel rumored to be arriving on next year’s successor.

At $900 — or potentially more, considering this tablet actually launched at $850 — the Legion Tablet’s hardware leaves something to be desired. Biometrics are the most obvious weak spot; camera-based face unlock is the only biometric option provided here, without a fingerprint scanner in sight. I wouldn’t blame some if they saw this as a dealbreaker, because even if you’re willing to put up with the security concerns that a basic front-facing camera brings to the table, I can promise you you’ll be typing the code in all the time. Whether you’re trying to unlock in a darker environment or it’s just been four hours since you last unlocked the slate, make sure you have your pin memorized.

If you’re primarily buying this as a content consumption machine, I think you’ll mostly have a great time. Lenovo built stereo sound into this slate, but did so in one of the smartest ways I’ve ever seen, ensuring all speakers are located to the right side along the bottom and top of the device. This might sound a little unbalanced in portrait mode, but in landscape, it guarantees you’re never actually covering up the speakers while holding the slate in your hands, something practically every other equivalent tablet is guilty of. No headphone jack here, unfortunately, something I would’ve liked to have seen on a gaming-focused device.

I find battery life genuinely difficult to judge on tablets, especially if you don’t pick it up every single hour of every single day, but I’ve been impressed overall with the Legion Tab’s longevity. Some weekend YouTube binge watching sessions at relatively high brightness settings left me with plenty of juice in the tank, and its standby time between sessions has been excellent. Obviously, if you’re really pushing your graphical limits on this thing — or if you’re emulating non-native software through something like DroidDeck — you’re going to see a bit of a dip, but combined with fast charging and two USB-C ports for both portrait and landscape access, battery life gets a big thumbs-up from me.

Lenovo’s packed a couple of accessories in the box with this thing, but I wouldn’t get too excited. While it’s nice to see a 68W charger included for those aforementioned fast top-offs, the included folio case is just awful. Not only does the triangle-shaped flap barely stick together to form a proper stand, but one of the corners of my case was loose enough to frequently flex back and forth. Holding the tablet while wrapped in its case just felt bad, in the way that so many bundled cases often feel, and a quick look at Amazon shows that basically no recognizable brand — or unrecognizable, for that matter — has stepped up to offer something better.

The Legion Tablet also includes a screen protector in the box, if that’s how you roll.

Unsurprisingly, the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 in here can handle effectively anything you dare to throw at it. While my mobile games might be limited to more casual, indie fare like Balatro — and, by the by, if you’re still enjoying Balatro a couple of years later, the size and shape of this device makes it perfect — graphically-intense games played fine. Asphalt Legends or the HoYoverse games might not be my cup of tea, but they perform excellently on this device, and compared to the 12-inch tablets companies like Samsung and Amazon have become obsessed with, the display size here actually feels perfect.

We definitely have to talk about emulation, though, because it’s increasingly becoming the main focus of mobile gamers everywhere, and this feels like a tablet perfectly designed for something like DroidDeck. Getting Steam emulation — complete with the Deck’s usual Big Picture mode UI — available as an application on the Legion Tab Gen 5 takes all of two minutes and a handful of taps on your display, and I have to say, I’m pretty shocked at just how impressive the overall experience is right now.

DroidDeck gave me the option to bring my mini gaming tablet experience full-circle. While my Steam library has no shortage of games I think could run without stressing this slate, I wanted to push the envelope a little bit. Persona 3 Reload felt like as good a candidate as any: a modern title that doesn’t necessarily require quick response times and fits virtual controls quite nicely. Plus, most of my gaming time on Nvidia’s tablet a decade ago was spent working through Persona 3 Portable; like poetry, it rhymes. I installed the game, ran it on the Legion Tab, and to my surprise and delight, it was absolutely in a playable state.

Now, there are some caveats here. I did drop the game’s graphics preset to low, and even still, there were some occasional hiccups while running around an early dungeon. The game’s initial intros and disclaimers actually gave the impression the title wouldn’t run at all, but I was able to sneak up on a shadow, use a slash attack to begin the battle — basically the only thing in P3R that remotely requires accurate timing — and issue commands to my player character and party mates.

Obviously, your experience emulating Steam titles on the Legion Tab will vary on what you want to play, and with such wide variables between experiences, I probably wouldn’t push most gamers to run out and pick one up right away. It might be early days for DroidDeck, but considering how we’ve already seen it progress, I wouldn’t be surprised to see some buyers picking this up as a Valve-esque take on a gaming tablet.

With all of that power under the hood, though, it’s Lenovo’s take on Android that leaves a lot to be desired. It’s not just that this feels like a rough-and-ready take on AOSP, an unrefined package that would feel more in line with devices from a decade ago, though, yes, that’s half the struggle here. But at its worst, the Legion Tab Gen 5 simply feels unoptimized in daily use.

Scrolling through web pages or various apps often felt sluggish and heavy, like the UI elements on screen never actually match the movement of my finger, and it’s unclear how much of that was due to the refresh rate bug I described above. Auto-rotate was both super finnicky and super sluggish, alternating back and forth between one state or the other, and the auto-rotate button that pops up when it’s disabled would frequently fail to appear. Occasionally, I’d run into app issues, such as choppy playback on a 1440p YouTube video that got so bad — regardless of what resolution I selected — that I had to fully force close the app in settings to fix it. Even getting the slate to reliably wake up (or not wake up) when picking it up was annoying, as it’s simultaneously sensitive enough to frequently turn on when I don’t want it to, or to stay asleep when I’m trying to unlock it. Inevitably, I turned that setting off.

You might think that shelling out $900 for an Android tablet would buy you an out from pre-installed bloatware; you’d be wrong. During setup, the Legion Tab attempts to install a whole host of apps and games, including Perplexity, TikTok, Temu, several match-three games that I’ve truly never heard of, and no less than two mahjong and solitaire titles each. In fact, there might actually be three solitaire titles depending on what “Jigsawcard Solitaire Puzzle” is, but I unchecked all of these apps during setup and didn’t deem the title worthy of bothering to check.

While Lenovo has been trying to improve its software update policies on some recent devices, this slate isn’t among that group. To my knowledge, there is no official update schedule for this device, but based on past performance, I’d expect somewhere around 2 OS upgrades and 4 years of security patches, give or take.

I would’ve loved nothing more than to recommend this year’s Legion Tab to small tablet fans and gamers everywhere, but when this thing is $200 more than Apple’s latest iPad Mini — which in and of itself is absolutely overpriced — and $100 more than the base OLED Steam Deck post-price hike, I just have a hard time telling anyone to buy it. Really, its Steam performance was one of the few areas that made me feel truly excited by this thing, but it’s simply too unpredictable an experience at this point (and price) for me to recommend.

Even setting aside the price, there’s simply too much here that feels unfinished or rough around the edges for my liking. A handful of bug fixes and a couple of additional optimization passes could fix a lot of my more minor quibbles, but despite what I just said, you can only ignore the $900 price tag for so long before it bites you in the ass.

We have seen a post-iPad Mini discount bringing this slate to an Apple-matching $700 ahead of the holidays, but even that price is $150 more than its predecessor was at launch without a whole lot to show for it. If you’re looking for a gamer-friendly tiny tablet, I do think Legion is a brand worth keeping your eye on, especially as DroidDeck and other Steam emulation apps continue to evolve. But at this point — and for this price — your best bet is waiting for whatever model follows this one. It might still be stupid expensive, but at least you’ll be getting OLED.

A decade ago, Nvidia’s Shield Tablet felt like a no-brainer addition to my everyday carry. But in this economy, gamers and tablet fans alike are simply better off dropping $900 elsewhere.

A traditional bed slinger made mostly of LEGO; the printbed, leadscrews, and even the gantry are LEGO.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Adam Turaj, a Mechatronics Engineering student at the University of Waterloo, built an open-source LEGO 3D printer named “Studprint” with only 13 pieces of the printer not made out of LEGO. The bill of materials only totals $173.35, with $30 of the budget going to LEGO pieces that comprise 92% of the whole build. Turaj’s project got him flown to the Rocky Mountain RepRap Festival 2026, where he got to meet Prusa CMO Zack Freedman and presented Studprint to over 4,000 people at the event.

Earlier this year, Hack Club posted a challenge called Infill, calling makers and hobbyists to design their own 3D printers from scratch and receive a $350 grant to build their printers. Whoever submits a benchy with their printer gets a chance to be flown to the Rocky Mountain RepRap Festival 2026, and Turaj was one of them.

Turaj joined this challenge, designing his LEGO 3D printer in SOLIDWORKS. He named the project Studprint, referring to the studs on a LEGO brick. What takes this project even farther is that Turaj decided he would only use “classical LEGO,” avoiding LEGO Technic pieces wherever possible. Looking at the repository’s images of the CAD designs, you would easily mistake it for a virtual LEGO builder.

Turaj shared an image of the bill of materials (BOM) on the GitHub repository for his build, showing a final build price of $173.35. There are three major electronics components in the printer: the first is the BTT SKR Pico V1.0, a control board commonly used in open-source 3D printers like the Voron V0; for wireless capability, a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W is used; and the whole printer is powered by a Mean Well LRS-150-24 switching power supply — with all three components priced at around $25 each. This printer is built with the backbone of a true DIY 3D-printer build, unlike this cute LEGO 3D printer we covered last year that used a 3D printing pen.

There are five NEMA 17 stepper motors, also popular in 3D printers, whether open- or closed-source. Four of the motors control the axes, while the fifth is used to feed filament to the Trianglelab V6 Extruder. The rest of the 3D printer is made of $30 worth of LEGO pieces; even the build plate is a block of LEGO. Turaj’s only print shown on the GitHub repository is a Benchy, sliced in Klipper and printed in 1.25 hours; it’s surprisingly good considering the leadscrews are all LEGO pieces.

#10260. OpenAI board member makes a terrifying prediction: You will probably die from an AI accident

Anxieties around an AI doomsday have been ramping up for months, and executives at top AI companies have done little to ease those worries. OpenAI’s Sam Altman said humanity could lose control of the technology. Anthropic warned that its models could be abused to create chemical weapons.

But no AI leaders have looked people dead in the eye and said they specifically are going to be killed by artificial intelligence—until now.

Enter Paul Christiano, an OpenAI board member serving on its Safety and Security Committee. Earlier this week while speaking at the AI Safety Foundation’s annual Hinton Lectures, Christiano said he believes an AI takeover is imminent and that it spells certain doom for the human race.

“For most people in this room, the most likely reason they will die is because of an AI accident,” Christiano told the crowd.

What does an AI takeover mean to Christiano? He described it as “a situation where there are AI systems pursuing goals, and those systems call the shots in the same sense that humans today call the shots and what happens on Earth.”

“If, say, you or me or Donald Trump wanted to stop them, [we] would be as ineffective as if you or me were trying to stop the U.S. military,” he added.

Christiano’s AI timeline

How soon could humanity’s AI downfall happen? Christiano predicts it could occur within the next six months, or—somewhat more reassuringly?—take up to three years.

“If we tried to develop AI along the most rapid trajectory, if we said we’re just going to build this as quickly as we can in the easiest way we can, we would be looking at something like a coin flip of an AI takeover,” he reasoned.

On the bright side, Christiano said companies are avoiding that coin flip by pacing the frontier, as Anthropic’s Dario Amodei recommended after a former employee accused both Anthropic and OpenAI of “gambling with our lives.”

However, Christiano warns that “even with realistic policy responses, the risk remains exceptionally high.”

If anything, his outlook has grown slightly more urgent since joining OpenAI’s board in September. At the time, he estimated a 4% chance of losing control of AI within a year—double the six-month minimum he floated this week—and a 15% chance within three years (odds he acknowledged are based on his subjective beliefs).

“If we build superintelligence without more robust alignment, I expect we will permanently lose control of it,” Christiano wrote in a personal statement. “If that happens then most people could die. I believe we would need domestic and international coordination to ensure global consistency and reduce risk to an acceptable level.”

#10258. A remote employee refused 160 webcam photos a day. Her employer fired her

Across the workforce, employer surveillance is growing increasingly common, even though it is widely disliked by employees. According to the American Psychological Association, employee monitoring increases workers’ stress and decreases their reported mental health. A Canadian study found that surveillance in the workplace makes employees feel more pressured, less satisfied with their job, and like their privacy is being violated.

AI may now make this problem worse. These negative outcomes are the consequences of more traditional surveillance methods like keyboard tracking and email monitoring. Considering that, what would the psychological impact be of learning that an employer will now use AI to take 160 photos of an employee’s face every day?

A recent New Jersey lawsuit alleges that an employer was trying to do just that, and fired its employee when she refused to agree to this monitoring. The plaintiff in this case, Glennis Von Sander-Timinski, worked for Sutherland Healthcare Solutions, which provides healthcare services outsourcing. The suit states that she had been working at home with no issues since 2018, and had achieved positive performance reviews during that time. 

However, everything changed in August when her company told her that they would be using a new tool: Sentinel AI. This software would take a photo of her through her webcam about every three minutes over the course of the day, for a total of about 160 photos per day.

Von Sander-Timinski objected to this with the worry that it would increase her stress level, and therefore trigger her underlying lupus. According to the Lupus Foundation of America, stress can be a significant trigger of lupus flares, which can result in fevers, rashes, and sores. Her doctor wrote a note to her employer arguing that the facial AI monitoring should be changed to be “intermittent or less frequently, as it is causing worsening of anxiety and flaring her systemic lupus erythematosus.”

However, Sutherland Healthcare was not willing to compromise and gave her an ultimatum. She could agree to the AI monitoring, come into the office every day, or be fired. Returning to the office was not feasible as she lives in Atlantic County, on the opposite side of New Jersey from her employer’s office in Clinton. The lawsuit estimated that her daily commute would have been a total of six hours long.

Therefore, on September 8, Von Sander-Timinski was fired. She had worked at Sutherland for over a decade, since it acquired the company she previously worked for in 2013. 

“Our client’s employer failed to engage in the interactive process required under the New Jersey Law Against Discrimination and denied a reasonable accommodation that would have allowed Ms. Von Sander-Timinski to continue performing her job duties successfully, as she had done for years prior to the implementation of this monitoring system,” said Von Sander-Timinski’s lawyers in a statement to The Bergen Record.

While many states currently do not have any laws against employer surveillance, some states, such as New York, Connecticut, Delaware, and California, are beginning to set boundaries for companies. Earlier this year, Maine also passed a law that bans surveillance within an employee’s home unless it is deemed necessary.

New Jersey is similarly looking to pass a law that would regulate AI electronic monitoring tools in the workplace. It would mandate that AI-powered surveillance would need to be approved by an independent auditor and would limit where and when monitoring can be active. 

While this bill is still under discussion, it could potentially help employees like Von Sander-Timinski avoid similar situations in the future. For now, in the vast majority of states, if an employer decides to implement facial monitoring, employees will have little option but to smile for the camera.

The plaque commemorates that shared history.America’s Diner has long been a place where people and ideas come together, and that history deserves to be preserved.”

Jensen Huang was one of the American success stories in Silicon Valley, where he had his humble beginnings as a seasonal dishwasher, busboy, and waiter at his nearby Denny’s before he rose to stardom as the head of Nvidia. The diner honored this achievement with a plaque at the booth where Jensen Huang, Chris Malachowsky, and Curtis Priem met after their working hours and first planned the inception of Nvidia. However, NBC News said that the sign has since been removed following Huang’s spectacular fall from grace and resignation from the company.

Unfortunately, employees say that the commemorative plaque, which read, “The booth that launched a $1 trillion company,” has been removed. It remains unclear who ordered the removal, though, so we reached out to Denny’s for comment and will update the story if they answer.

Despite being a billionaire, the former Nvidia CEO is known for keeping in touch with his roots. He has been spotted several times eating street food and enjoying local fast food in the various cities that he visits. He even once dragged the 35 Taiwanese industry chiefs to a restaurant in Taipei, earning that event the moniker “trillion-dollar banquet.” This “man of the people” persona has made him quite a popular figure among some people, fueling the Jensanity hype, especially in his home country of Taiwan.

We also saw this side of Jensen during the unveiling of the plaque in 2023, after Nvidia hit a $1 trillion valuation, when he balanced 10 plates and served food during the event. The restaurant also put up a food truck and served “Nvidia Breakfast Bytes” at GTC 2025, which consisted of four sausage links served with four buttermilk silver dollar pancakes and some syrup, and was available for a limited time for under $5 in all Denny’s branches across the country.

There is no telling yet what’s next for Jensen Huang. Elon Musk has reportedly offered him a position, saying that it “would be an honor” to hire the person who was arguably one of the biggest driving forces in today’s AI industry, but he’s also facing numerous investigations from both his company, Congress, and the FBI. #10254. FAA grounds all flights in the U.S. until further notice: Reports cite air traffic control outage

In a rare move, the Federal Aviation Administration said Friday that it was grounding all flights in the United States from departing “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety . . . until further notice,” according to NBC News.

The FAA reportedly issued the ground stop “due to several impacts to ATC [air traffic control] Frequencies and/or Radar capabilities,” with the FAA command center telling airlines it does not have further information on the “timing or cause of this outage,” aviation industry news service The Air Current reported.

Reached by Fast Company, the FAA pointed to a post on X from Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy, saying the ground stop “follows a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers.”

Duffy added: “FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them.”

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters at the White House, “there is no indication that we’ve had, no reason to believe, that as of right now this was a threat to the United States,” later adding, “this was a telecommunication outage,” per CNN.

According to FlightAware.com, a live flight tracker website, there are more than 9,000 flights delayed within, into, or out of the U.S. today, with 440 flights canceled (as of 5:20 p.m. ET).

“Every flight has been accounted for and international flights will be handled on a case by case basis,” the FAA posted on X.

The last nationwide ground stop was on January 11, 2023, when a contractor for the FAA “unintentionally deleted files related to a key pilot safety system,” according to CNN reporting at that time. The only other time such an order was issued was following the attacks on September 11, 2001.

Several methods can help you deal with online threats and strengthen security. All are effective, but each has a trade-off. For example, the harder you make it for bots to affect your website’s performance, the more likely you are to frustrate real customers.

Those of you who browse online daily know that credential stuffing, fake signups & payment fraud keep growing. To prevent fraud, businesses install CAPTCHAs & hard blocks that treat bots and legitimate users the same, diverting them to your competitors.

IP geolocation maps an IP address to a physical location & network details, letting you spot suspicious traffic before it reaches sensitive actions. Used well, it’s an invisible, low-friction risk signal. In this guide, you will learn how to flag high-risk activity and apply soft geo-fencing with step-up authentication.

Today, an IP lookup returns far more than a country & city. It can also reveal several other parameters, like

Each of these fields acts as a clue telling who is really behind a request.

This data powers anomaly detection. You can start by building a baseline for normal behavior for each user with aspects like

Then, you can watch for deviations from that pattern. An attacker won’t look like the account’s real owner, so you'll catch them.

Geolocation makes several common attack patterns easy to spot:

The first is traffic bursts from data center ASNs. These are bots, as real customers don’t browse from cloud servers

Many accounts created from one IP or subnet. This is a clear sign of fake signups

Impossible travel, such as logins from two distant locations within minutes

Timezone vs. IP mismatch. A device’s clock disagrees with its apparent location.

Note: Geolocation is just a signal, not a verdict. VPNs, travel, & mobile carriers can all create false alarms, so it works best when combined with other signals. That’s exactly why a proportional, soft response beats a hard block.

In short, IP geolocation turns a bare IP address into context, helping you separate real users from automated or fraudulent traffic.

Not every IP geolocation anomaly deserves the same response. The simplest way to stay consistent is to define a clear risk-signal framework.

That can be a short list of checks. Each check can have a weight that reflects how strongly it suggests fraud.

With risk scoring, you can turn these checks into a decision. You just have to assign each signal a numeric weight.

For example, medium can be 10 & 30 can be high.

Now, you need to add up every signal that comes up & map the total to thresholds like

A single medium signal passes quietly, but several can trigger action.

If you treat this as an automatic block, it would punish legitimate customers. Instead, let it raise the score & you take action only if it stacks with other signals, like a hosting IP or a new device.

Now that you know how to quantify the risk, here is how you can protect yourself without damaging UX.

Before soft, let us learn about hard blocking. This is where you completely deny or permanently ban traffic from specific geographic regions.

Now, hard blocking by country may look effective, but it can backfire quickly. Here is how.

In the worst case, determined bot operators simply rotate to IPs in allowed regions, so the only people you stop are your real customers.

This is where the balance between security and user experience becomes critical. As the digital strategist and Founder at LawRank, Mariano Rodriguez emphasizes, "Your website's security should be a silent guardian, not a roadblock. If your fraud prevention creates friction, you aren't just stopping bots—you're turning away real clients. True digital trust is built when backend protections are seamless and invisible to the legitimate user."

Now, with soft geo-fencing, you can respond to risk proportionally instead of making a simple allow-or-deny call. Instead of totally banning the users, you adjust the level of friction to match the risk score from the previous section:

**Note: **For soft geo-fencing, passkeys are safest because they are phishing-resistant. Only a legitimate user can take the biometric tap and pass.

Before we start, let’s understand Express.js middleware. An Express.js middleware for Geolocation Risk Scores is a custom or 3rd party function that intercepts the incoming HTTP requests, extracts the client's IP address, fetches a security risk profile based on their geographic location & attaches that data to the request object (req) before it reaches your route handlers.

Here is how you can use it for fraud prevention and bot mitigation:

Note: You can make it stronger by adding velocity checks (too many attempts from one IP or account) & device fingerprints.

From a broader angle, IP geolocation isn't the final verdict. It is just a signal. But with this signal, you can score each request, respond in proportion to the risk & save hard blocks for clear abuse. This increases the friction for bots and keeps the flow easy for legitimate users.

#10252. Apple TV has a new ASL feature, offering a richer language experience beyond captions

Apple introduced a new sign language interpretation feature on Friday, alongside the premiere of the Apple TV movie Being Heumann.

The feature, designed with native signers, offers a visual of a person on the screen. Rather than replacing captions as an accessibility option, Apple is offering another function to improve users’ viewing experience through American Sign Language and British Sign Language.

People in the Deaf community have cited inability to get the full experience of watching shows and movies due to captions that lack descriptions of tone and mood. Poorly timed captions can throw off an entire episode or movie, and incorrect language can alter the understanding of a conversation.

The new feature goes hand in hand with the 2026 biographical drama directed by Sian Heder based on the memoir Being Heumann: An Unrepentant Memoir of a Disability Rights Activist by its namesake Judith Heumann with writer Kristen Joiner.

Starring Mark Ruffalo and Dylan O’Brien, and Ruth Madeley as Heumann, the film debuted in select theaters on November 6 and was released for streaming on Apple TV today. 

A 2021 Census Bureau presentation discussed the difficulty of collecting accurate ASL-user statistics through traditional household language surveys. The Deaf community is often undercounted in national data, making it harder to measure accessibility needs. 

Apple Originals have led the industry in providing accessibility features, such as Subtitles for the Deaf and Hard of Hearing and Audio Description for blind and low-vision audiences, in multiple languages, worldwide. 

For its new feature, Apple created each interpretation with a DASL (director of artistic sign language) and an interpreter. They worked together in a studio to create high-quality sign language, capturing the tone and emotional intensity of each film being interpreted.

“I’m proud to have been part of Being Heumann and thrilled to see Apple TV supporting greater accessibility for Deaf audiences,” said Daniel Durant, who appears in the movie and also directed the film’s sign language interpretation.

#10251. The iPhone Duo’s rocky launch is a reminder of how far Android foldables have come

Good morning. Today I’m finding open source alternatives to all of my apps, poring through Pitchfork’s list of the 100 best indie rock albums to find ones I haven’t listened to, and preparing my body for November 19th by pre-loading GTA VI (and replaying GTA IV in the meantime).

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.

On Monday, I unboxed the iPhone Duo I pre-ordered back in October and experienced a disarming sense of déjà vu. It’s beautiful hardware married to a messy, often painful software onboarding experience atypical of Apple’s usual polish. It reminds me of the Galaxy Fold’s early years.

I was most looking forward to the combination of a foldable form factor and Apple’s superior app ecosystem, but even the apps that have been updated to support the new aspect ratio, on both the front and back, feel ungainly and buggy. In moving UI elements from the bottom to the right, even with the display open, the Duo forces a rebuilding of essential muscle memory that’s prevailed across mobile platforms, including Android foldables, for 20 years.

The front display, in particular, is a massive test of one’s patience: apps, even ones ostensibly optimized for its stout dimensions, often feel unusable, with UI elements that would be prominent on the iPhone 18 Pro hidden behind overflow menus on the Duo. It’s exasperating and, frankly, boggling.

But what’s interesting is the enthusiasm with which developers are approaching the new form factor. Reddit threads reveal dozens of Duo-optimized app recommendations that feel novel and, if not polished, then propulsive. There’s a fascinating delta between waiting for my bank, or Starbucks, or Kobo, to get its act together to support the Duo and seeking out net-new opportunities and experiences.

I spent most of the summer using the Galaxy Z Fold 8, and I didn’t expect going back to it to feel so stately and predictable: the showcase of a platform with fewer highs but none of the Duo’s current lows.

I’m not sure if I’m going to keep the Duo and wait out its colicky infancy. But I do know that until now I hadn’t given Samsung enough credit for the amount of work it did to make foldable software feel ordinary, and that’s the highest compliment I can pay.

This section has some of our favorite stuff from around the internet. Great videos, weird memes, fun reads, recommended apps, whatever. Send us your recommendations!

Andrew’s look at the Boox Picco is a nice reminder that a gadget can be interesting because it does less. The $109 e-reader has a 4-inch screen, physical page-turn buttons, and an included magnetic case that can attach to a compatible phone. It competes directly with XTEINK’s excellent X4 Pro, which features a rudimentary touchscreen and backlight for around $100, though its magnets are built in.

Both products are wonderful examples of hardware companies adapting to the growing size and complexity of smartphones and seeing an opening for single-purpose products that do one thing really well. Plus, it’s fun to stick a thing to the back of your phone and… read it.

For something you can explore without buying another device, Paolo Mainardi turned his personal website into a point-and-click adventure. Articles live in books, links sit on a notice board, and his about page is a letter in a lighthouse. The Context Island is an incredibly thoughtful and unique approach to “web” design, and it’s another example of how AI can really help bring crazy ideas to fruition.

We’ll likely find out today whether Jensen Huang will be removed as Nvidia’s CEO. According to the WSJ, the company’s board is preparing to oust the company’s singular chief executive, who co-founded it in 1993.

Momentum picked up after the New York Times reported that in addition to his three-year affair with Alice Huang, an alleged Chinese spy, Jensen had a relationship with one of his direct reports, who still works at the company.

This won't magically bring units to 100% health, but it should increase survival rates for wounded soldiers in the frontlines.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A Chinese military medical school has just developed a UAV that could remotely administer medicine, helping treat injured soldiers on the front lines without putting medical personnel at risk. According to Chinese mouthpiece Global Times, the Air Force Medical University built the first casualty-search drone for the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) that fires darts loaded with painkillers to help ease the pain of wounded personnel.

“We have developed the military’s first casualty-search drone and have also made some breakthroughs in treatment. For example, we can use drones to inject medication into wounded personnel from a considerable distance,” Air Force Medical University representative Wang Jianqi told the publication. “Wherever our drone can fly, we can deliver life-saving emergency medication into a wounded person’s muscle, buying valuable time for treatment.”

Russia’s invasion of Ukraine saw the widespread use of drones on the frontline, primarily for search-and-destroy and reconnaissance missions. However, the four-year escalation of the 12-year war has seen the creative implementations of these units — from jam-proof fiber optic drones to the use of heavy-lift hexacopters for medical evacuation. Now, drones-as-first-responders are being developed for civilian use, including firefighting drones, camera response drones, and even “Campus Guardian Angel” drones designed to neutralize school shooters.

However, China's air-ground treatment drone remains in the experimental stage, says Wang. After all, you can’t just administer medication without assessing the patient’s vital signs and their injuries. It’s also difficult or even impossible to load an incapacitated soldier without external assistance. Still, the deployment of medical UAVs would help with battlefield medicine, which has developed the concept of the “golden hour,” which suggests that wounded personnel treated within the first hour have the greatest chance of survival.

Although battlefield medicine was in use since the 1800s, especially during Napoleon’s invasion of Russia and the American Civil War, helicopter medevacs were first deployed during World War 2 in Burma and the Philippines. The Korean War saw the introduction of MASH — Mobile Army Surgical Hospital — units that brought forward treatment units closer to the frontline.

This, combined with the widespread use of UH-1 Hueys during the Vietnam War to evacuate wounded soldiers from the front lines, sometimes while under enemy fire, has greatly increased the survival rate among wounded soldiers. Today, helicopter and ground medevacs are common among military forces, with drone treatment and evacuation now being experimented with in both the frontlines of Ukraine and military medical universities in China.

This tip originally appeared in the free Cool Tools newsletter from The Intelligence. Get the next issue in your inbox and get ready to discover all sorts of awesome tech treasures!

The simplest QR code creator

A little refresher before getting to the tool itself: QR codes are those square-shaped barcodes full of little pixelated squares and a set of larger markers in the corners. You might see them in restaurants (“Leave us a review on Yelp!”), from street vendors collecting Venmo payments, or as part of the setup process for a smart home device. Most of the time, scanning them just opens a link to a web page without your having to type anything.

➜ For a simple, straightforward way to create your own QR codes with ease, check out Ente QR, a free website with no sign-ups or usage limits.

⌚ Generating a code takes mere seconds, and only a few minutes longer if you want to customize the look.

There are any number of reasons why you might find it helpful to create QR codes of your own. I keep an image file with a QR code handy on my phone, for instance, to let folks easily sign up for my newsletters. You could also have a QR code that links to your website on business cards, a printout of one that points people to a shared digital photo album for your next party, or to a page with your Wi-Fi password and other details for house guests.

✅ Whatever you want to use it for, Ente QR lets you create a code with a few simple steps:

  • Paste a link into the address field.
  • Tweak the color and visual style of the QR code.
  • Click the download button to get the QR code image as a PNG image file.

The site’s customization features strike the right balance between simplicity and utility, with a handful of dot formatting options and preset colors, plus a color picker if you want something specific. There’s also a “Logo” option that embeds an image in the middle of the QR code.

Ente says the QR code creation runs entirely in your browser, and the codes always lead directly to the link you included, with no creepy tracking in between. It’s a side project from a company that mainly works on private photo and document storage. 

The biggest limitation is that Ente’s QR codes are only for linking to web addresses. If you want to create a QR code for sharing plain text, a prefilled email, or a digital contact card, BlockSurvey’s privacy-focused QR code generator is a good alternative. While it’s not as stylish as Ente QR, it supports more data formats—but for most people’s purposes, Ente more than fits the bill.

  • Ente QR is available in any browser and works well on both desktop and mobile devices.
  • It’s free to use with no ads, sign-ups, subscriptions, or usage limits.
  • Ente does not track the URLs in the QR codes you create and does not set tracking cookies on its website.

#10246. A New York Times writer spent an hour trying to reach Walmart. Then she deleted her account and told the world

When your AI tool for customer service causes so much frustration that it’s featured in the nation’s largest newspaper, you know you’ve got a problem. That’s where Walmart finds itself this week. 

The leading brick-and-mortar retailer, and second-biggest company on earth by revenue (recently edged out by Amazon), left a New York Times writer with no choice but to cancel her Walmart account altogether.

The story of what happened is instructive. So is the solution. There’s an easy way to avoid this problem. And small businesses that do so are in a position to grab market share from the giants in their fields.

‘Over an hour attempting to get help from a human’

Ivy Liscomb is a writer for Wirecutter, an independent review site that’s part of the Times. She recently shared her all-too-familiar story of contacting a company for a customer service issue and getting caught in an endless AI loop. 

Walmart no longer carried a product she wanted, so she tried to cancel her delivery subscription online. But there was no button to do so. So she called customer support. “A bright, automated voice insisted that I could cancel my subscription online, even after I explained that I couldn’t. At some point, Walmartbot appeared to accept that I was ‘experiencing a glitch.’ And then it dropped the bomb: I could reload the page and try again, or delete my Walmart account.”

She set about trying the usual methods to get a real person on the phone—saying the right word or phrase, pressing the right buttons, even hanging up and calling back. “Finally, after spending over an hour attempting to get help from a human, I deleted my account. In an age of countless digital storefronts vying for my cart, it seemed unbelievable that such a successful brand would allow faulty AI to cost it a customer.”

She’s far from alone. Recent surveys show how critical this issue is: 87% of consumers “say it is essential for companies to provide an option to reach a human agent when using genAI,” Gartner reported. And just this week, Consumer Cellular released results of its survey of consumers 50 and older: More than 80% said they’d consider leaving a company if its automated system kept them in a loop.

Escalation is table stakes

None of this should scare companies away from using AI for the customer experience (CX). In fact, people increasingly like interfacing with AI. In the Gartner survey, half of consumers said their interactions are even easier with generative AI than they are with humans.

The key is to establish simple, rapid methods for people to break out of AI. This takes the right programming. CX tools are designed to be helpful. They’re taught to handle as many queries as possible autonomously. Usually, this pays off. They process huge amounts of data so rapidly that there’s often very little wait to bring customers from one step to the next.

But that benefit becomes a drawback when things go awry. Many AI receptionists prioritize solving problems for customers, so they keep searching for a way to do so even when they can’t find one. Think of it as a “never give up” attitude taken to an extreme.

The best AI receptionists avoid this by establishing clear protocols for multistage escalation. First, when a customer starts to express any kind of frustration, a human agent is alerted. The person oversees the interaction and tries to guide the AI voice toward the right solution. If that doesn’t work, the call is transferred instantly to a human agent, with full context provided.

This clearly was not in place for Liscomb’s calls to Walmart. In fact, she wrote, not only did the Walmart AI bot rebuff her efforts to find a real person, it also forgot her issue after every few questions.

Small and medium-size businesses: See this as an opportunity. This CX gap in the marketplace provides you with the chance to win people over. Be the organizations that provide optimal AI tools and seamless access to real people. Provide the care and solution-oriented design that people crave. 

Customers are ready and willing to leave a brand if it doesn’t keep earning their business. With the right AI answering service, you can take the lead.

The opinions expressed here by Inc.com columnists are their own, not those of Inc.com.

—By Tomas Gorny, Co-founder and CEO, Nextiva

The upgrade costs speed: code output falls to 150–180 tokens per second, from 160–215.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A lawyer with a private AI server built on eight used Nvidia V100 GPUs returned with an update, moving about 80% of its work up from 2-bit to 4-bit NVFP4 precision and bringing in 1TB of RAM and an RTX 3090. The server uses DeepSeek V4.1 Flash with a legal harness, the workflows and checks he wraps around the model, for his law practice. The cost? Performance, with code output dropping from 160–215 to 150–180 tokens per second, although the crashes that hit the new build are gone. The culprit behind the crashes, originally blamed on PCIe, was likely a bad PSU.

Once a random hardware nerd lawyer on Reddit, the lawyer's responses to the original breaking story illuminated his identity. He’s a trial lawyer in Columbia, South Carolina. ProprietaryLegalAI commented on our first story three times, linking to a code repository, site, and LinkedIn that identify him as Nick Mermiges, founder of PLI Labs and proprietarylegal.ai. His other firm, PLI, is a technology consultancy, not a law firm, and now lists private, on-prem LLM serving as a service.

He built the software side with AI, specifically Claude Code, which wrote the kernels and ran the benchmarks with his direction. The Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.2 models handled the optimizations, custom kernels, and re-quantizing; he noted he was surprised at how well Fable built custom Volta kernels, and how it re-quantizes the experts his legal harness triggers. From about February to July, he built a legal harness around Claude that worked, while his attempts at a local-model version failed, but then DeepSeek V4.1 Flash arrived, and he was able to port it successfully, even if he says it’s not as good as frontier.

He reaffirms that “the documents never leave the office” and upgraded the system from 256GB to 1TB of RAM and tossed in a newer GPU, even as the V100s stay on “borrowed time” with R580, the last Nvidia driver branch to support them. The project’s intentions, as listed last time, suggested he wanted the system to be able to offload more of his workload, so this and the precision change are a reasonable upgrade. His previously stated goal of wanting the system to handle more than one request at a time has also been met.

The original “Volta sPLIt” build we covered has transformed into the “Volta Max uPLIft,” still with the clever lettering as his company’s initials are PLI — Proprietary Legal Intelligence. He now claims “near-NVFP4 precision,” having described NVFP4 on our forum earlier this week as “essentially full precision.” NVFP4 is Nvidia’s 4-bit floating-point format, and Nvidia publishes its own NVFP4 version of DeepSeek V4.1 Flash; the project’s README says that version matches the precision of the model’s official weights at 4.25 bits per weight.

DeepSeek V4.1 Flash is built from “experts,” the parts of the model that do most of the work for each word. This model didn’t fit at that precision before, as 384 routed experts, in each of 40 layers, counts to 15,360 in all. At official precision, this comes out to about 269 GiB, by his estimate, and eight 32GB V100s have 256 GiB in total before anything else is loaded. With the 2-bit build, the weights were 248.8GB; the new build’s Hugging Face package is about 556GB.

The workaround is to keep every expert on the cards at 2-bit and swap the most-used ones up until the cards are full, which in this case came out to about 38.7%, or 5,949 experts, at precisely NVFP4. “Most-used,” in this context, refers to a count from a mix of four kinds of text, which are weighted equally, one of which is his own legal harness traffic.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

The payoff is that those experts do most of the work. In testing with one request at a time, between 80% and 86% of decode routes, the calls to an expert made while the model writes, land on the NVFP4 experts, lowest for general text and highest for source code. The prediction for the two-request setup he runs is 78% to 85%. The remaining 15% to 22% of calls would still go to a 2-bit expert.

Measured against Nvidia’s own version of the model as the reference, he was able to get good results. Same next token, or how often a build picks the same next token as the reference, went up to 95.1% from 92.2%. For KL divergence, which measures how far a build’s probabilities are from the reference’s, it went down to 0.079 nats from 0.196. In measuring multiple-choice answers that change, across 513 questions from a standard multiple-choice knowledge test, it went from 79 different to just 8.

This does not measure accuracy — which was about the same across all three cases — but fidelity. Those tests ran on the build’s first release, but not on the new two-request setup he now runs.

The result of the changes: higher fidelity but at a lower level of performance. Code output is 3% to 30% slower, depending on the prompt length, and legal writing is 9% to 23% slower. Before the build, he hoped to maintain about 80 tokens per second on legal and prose; the bench came in at 86 to 106 for legal and 78 to 86 for prose. The upside is that running two requests at once raises total output to 159.0 tokens per second, versus 118.9 with a sole request. The first token also arrives sooner at every prompt length, 108.4 seconds versus 118.7 seconds at 256K tokens.

Each request needs a “slot,” though, and this comes at a cost. Every slot keeps its own state on the cards, which leaves room for fewer NVFP4 experts: 6,215, 5,949, 5,663 for one, two, and three slots, respectively. This means each added slot may push another one to two points of the calls back to 2-bit, which could reduce output quality.

Legal writing (tokens/s), 2-bit / near-NVFP4

Builder’s measurements, Nov. 5 (2-bit) and Nov. 12 (near-NVFP4); greedy decoding, thinking off, one request at a time.

The move to more RAM came this week with eight 128GB modules at 2,933 MT/s, originally eight 32GB modules that had to be run at DDR4-2666 due to ECC errors. After the RAM upgrade, the host reports two NUMA nodes, and two boots hung at the first transfer between the boards, so he reordered the cards in software. The GPUs remain capped at 1,522 MHz, as before.

As for the PSU, he took the common approach of chasing PCIe slots, cards, and cables to narrow down the cause, finally concluding it was “probably one bad PSU.” He also added more fans, but with no temperature changes, this only indicated that airflow was not the problem. He changed the power delivery, and nine of nine long chats read clean afterward. Also, don’t judge his cable management skill; any “advice [there] is welcome and will be ignored,” which is the only comment to make in that situation.

He also already has two DGX Sparks running the same model at 1M context for agent work, and three or four sessions at once, and he isn’t stopping there. Now it comes down to scaling. Eight more V100s and a second server, with 512GB of 3,200 MT/s ECC RAM, are waiting in the wings. The second box would run another high-precision DeepSeek, used as an extra agent or to run tasks in parallel. The plan is also to move DeepSeek’s small draft model off the V100s and onto the RTX 3090, which hasn’t happened yet.

#10243. Don’t buy the new Apple TV 4K until Apple does these 3 things

I’m a huge fan of Apple’s digital media player, the Apple TV 4K. I’ve owned every version of the Apple TV for over a decade now, and have used Apple’s Movies store to purchase hundreds of films.

The diminutive Apple TV 4K is my sole portal to my television, and it easily beats other media streamers—including those from Roku, Amazon, and Google—when it comes to ease of use and user interface.

Like many, I had been eagerly waiting for a new Apple TV 4K, ready to upgrade. Apple’s last version came out back in 2022, and though it still works perfectly fine, I was excited to see what new modern features and improvements the 2026 model would have.

But the 2026 model, which went on sale on Friday, November 13—it kills me to say—is a letdown. The hardware is fantastic, but the device is failed by its software. And its price is double that of its predecessor. For the first time since I began buying Apple TVs more than a decade ago, I’ll be sitting this model out—and you probably should, too—until Apple does these three things.

Fixes its TV app

The worst thing about the Apple TV, ironically, has always been its TV app. That’s the app you use to access the Apple TV streaming service, as well as all the movies and TV shows you’ve purchased from the iTunes Store.

I’ve written in detail about the TV app before, and unfortunately its weakness remains, even in tvOS 27, the operating system that powers the new Apple TV 4K. It’s so barebones that it feels like the development team behind it created it as an afterthought.

The actual video playback of the TV app is fine. It’s got a nice Liquid Glass sheen and is pretty fluid. But it’s also, ostensibly, designed to be the home for all your digital entertainment—how you access all the movies and series you’ve purchased through the iTunes Store. And it’s horrible at that.

The most egregious failure (and there are many) of the TV app is that it still doesn’t offer the basic functionality of letting users organize their purchased movies and series into collections for easy categorization on the Apple TV 4K. And this is sorely needed, because the built-in Genre categories the app does offer so often misclassify or outright omit movies that it seems like a sin against cinema itself.

Adds missing apps

A second frustration with the Apple TV 4K is that it is still lacking two apps all other Apple devices support—and these apps are perfect for a television.

One is a dedicated Home app, as you have on the iPhone, iPad, Mac, and even the Apple Watch. Apple positions the Apple TV 4K as one of the central hubs of your smart home, so it’s baffling that the company hasn’t ported its Home app to it, which would let you monitor and control your security feeds and smart devices from the comfort of your couch. 

Then there is the Weather app. Apple’s Weather app is the most beautiful out there, thanks to rich graphics that visually represent local conditions. And, you know, for some 70 years now, people have been conditioned to tune into their TVs to get their local weather forecast. So why does the Apple TV, after all these years, still not have a dedicated Weather app that you can access with a click of the Siri Remote?

Expands its gaming capabilities

In advance of the new Apple TV 4K announcement, many people, including myself, speculated (and indeed, hoped) that Apple would finally turn the Apple TV 4K into a true gaming console. But when Apple released the new unit, with the powerful A19 chip inside, the company didn’t announce any new gaming capabilities to go with it.

This was surprising, since the new A19 chip is more than capable of running AAA console games, unlike the A15 chip in the prior-generation Apple TV 4K. I mean, even the A17 Pro chip in the iPhone 15 Pro, which is inferior to the A19, can run AAA titles like the Resident Evil 2 remake, Assassin’s Creed Mirage, Red Dead Redemption, Control: Ultimate Edition, Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas, and more.

Of all these gripes, the new Apple TV 4K’s lack of gaming enhancements is the most disappointing, considering that it costs $299, twice the price of the previous model with 128GB of storage, and now nearly as much as a Nintendo Switch.

Apple should have compensated users for that massive price hike—which, admittedly, was likely due to increased memory costs that were outside the company’s control—with the software enhancements above, which are entirely within Apple’s control.

At $149, these historic omissions were annoying but tolerable. At $299, they’re deal-breakers. And if you’ve got an existing Apple TV 4K, there’s no compelling reason to upgrade until Apple changes course.

#10241. Here’s how to fix the looming Social Security shortfall

The Social Security Board of Trustees announced earlier this year that everyone’s favorite government program can pay 100% of scheduled benefits until the fourth quarter of 2032. After that, the Social Security Trust Fund will be depleted, and we will only have enough money to pay a little over three-quarters of promised benefits.

(Cue the collective cynical shrug from Generation X, which has learned not to count on nice things.)

This imminent shortfall is hardly a surprise—the Social Security Administration (SSA) has been forecasting the depletion of the Trust Fund and the corresponding inability to pay out 100% of scheduled benefits for at least 16 years. Which is why the government’s refusal to propose any solutions before we run out the insolvency clock is the leading cause of ulcers in actuaries, people planning to retire in the next 10 years, and your Uncle Leo.

While there are a number of possible Social Security fixes, each one has the potential to seriously tick off various groups. That’s why we may not see real proposals for solving the shortfall until we’ve nearly hit the deadline (which is what happened back in 1983 when Social Security amendments were implemented mere weeks before the money ran out). It’s also entirely possible that Congress will enact Band-Aids that kick the issue down the road rather than solve the problem for the long term.

Understanding the most commonly proposed solutions is one of the best things you can do to help hurry along the process of fixing Social Security. Here’s what you need to know about how we might eliminate the Social Security shortfall.

How the program currently works

Social Security is more than 90 years old, which means that probably every single person reading this has never known a world without it. When a program is that deeply entrenched, it’s easy to miss important details about how it operates—and understanding the mechanics is the first step to understanding potential fixes.

To start, most Social Security funding comes from a 12.4% payroll tax on earned income, with the employee and employer each contributing 6.2%. Social Security works as a direct handover from current workers to current beneficiaries—but in years the SSA collected more in taxes than it paid out in benefits, the excess was invested in government debt (like Treasury bonds), with a guaranteed minimum interest rate of 3%. This excess is called the Social Security Trust Fund, and it’s the money that is currently running out.

Under the current system, we don’t have enough workers paying enough money into the system to ensure that beneficiaries in 2033 and beyond will receive 100% of the benefits promised to them.

What we can adjust

There are only three levers we can pull to cover the imminent shortfall:

  • Increase the amount of money paid into the program.
  • Increase the number of workers.
  • Decrease benefits.

Unfortunately, each option comes with unpopular disadvantages that could make it a political nonstarter. But if Americans understand how adjusting these three aspects of Social Security funding would work, we’ll be in a better position to negotiate a mix of solutions that will satisfy (or at least not enrage) everyone.

Increasing money paid into the program

If you’re running out of money, getting more is typically the most obvious solution to the problem. And there are several proposals for how to do this.

Raise the payroll tax

Currently, workers and employers each pay 6.2% in payroll taxes toward Social Security, for a total tax percentage of 12.4%. (Anyone who is self-employed is on the hook for the full 12.4%.)

Raising the payroll tax to 8.4% for both workers and employers—a combined rate of 16.8%—would completely eliminate the shortfall for 75 years. But getting Americans to agree to this kind of tax hike—even if it’s implemented in small stages over time—sounds about as likely as mastering time travel.

Eliminate the taxable maximum

The SSA sets an annual taxable base rate that rises every year based on average wage growth. As of 2026, this taxable maximum is set at $184,500. (It increases to $192,300 in 2027.) You pay Social Security taxes on every dollar you earn up to that base rate, but not above it.

That means the maximum anyone pays in Social Security taxes in 2026 is $11,439 (6.2% of $184,500), while their employer pays the same amount. In other words, an engineer earning $200,000 and Elon Musk both pay the same amount into Social Security.

Eliminating the taxable maximum amount could eliminate up to 73% of the Social Security shortfall for the next 75 years, according to a 2021 report by the Congressional Research Service. (The numbers may have changed somewhat in the five years since this report was published, but it remains true that getting rid of the taxable maximum will cover a large portion of the shortfall over the next three-quarters of a century.)

While this potential solution would probably gain traction among the 94% of the population whose income is below the annual taxable base rate, the 6% with higher incomes tend to have outsize political power.

Increasing the number of workers

Whether or not we tinker with the percentage of taxes paid or the taxable maximum, more workers would also help Social Security’s cash flow. But where will these new workers come from?

Raise the birth rate

To keep a stable population, a country must maintain a total fertility rate of 2.1 children for every woman. America’s fertility rate has been declining, recording its lowest-ever rate in 2024 with 1.6 births per woman. In addition to disappointing huge swaths of would-be grandparents, a declining birth rate also means we have fewer and fewer workers to pay into Social Security as those babies grow up.

Increasing America’s fertility rate would be a long-term solution to Social Security’s financial woes, but there are several stumbling blocks. The biggest is that it would take multiple decades for any initiative we enact to show up in Social Security funding. Additionally, the kinds of programs that encourage fertility, such as paid parental leave and subsidized childcare, can be politically controversial.

Encourage immigration

Immigrants, including legal residents and those who are undocumented, are a net benefit to the Social Security program. That’s because immigrants pay into the system via payroll taxes, just like any other workers, while a significant portion are not eligible to receive benefits later in life.

Since immigrants are more likely to be of working age when they arrive in the U.S., encouraging more immigration gives the economy the same boost as a higher birth rate 25 or 30 years ago. The Center on Budget and Policy Priorities reports that if annual net immigration were roughly 400,000 more people, it would reduce Social Security’s shortfall by 11%.

But immigration has been a political flashpoint for a very long time, which makes this solution a difficult one to implement.

Decreasing benefits

While no one likes the idea of reducing benefits, it is one way to lower Social Security’s costs. Although it’s exceedingly unlikely that the SSA would ever reduce benefits for current beneficiaries, there are some proposals that may affect future benefits.

Raise the retirement age

Currently, full retirement age—the age when you are entitled to your full Social Security retirement benefits—is set between 66 and 67, depending on your birth year. You may take benefits as early as 62, but the amount you receive is permanently reduced by approximately 8% per year between age 62 and your full retirement age.

Congress has already increased the retirement age once. In 1983, recognizing that the baby boom generation would begin retiring en masse as of 2011, Congress incrementally increased full retirement from age 65 to 67. This made the boomers’ retirement less expensive for Social Security, as they either received lower payments if they claimed benefits before the new retirement age, or they waited longer.

Life expectancy in the U.S. has increased over time, meaning Social Security has been asked to provide benefits for a longer period. Some experts recommend increasing the retirement age to 68 for Gen Z and/or Gen Alpha in order to reduce future costs.

However, life expectancy isn’t the same across all income levels. Lower-income workers have a shorter life expectancy and are less likely to live to retirement—and these workers also tend to rely more heavily on Social Security benefits when they do retire. Increasing the retirement age for these workers could harm the very citizens Social Security was created to protect.

Change the price index

Current Social Security beneficiaries receive an annual cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) to ensure their benefits maintain the same buying power throughout their retirement. COLA is calculated using the consumer price index (CPI), which measures the average change in prices for a basket of consumer goods.

But the CPI doesn’t account for elasticity of demand, which is a fancy way of saying that when prices go up, people change their spending habits. Which is why many experts recommend switching to the chained CPI for COLA calculations. This index accounts for spending substitutions in response to price changes, and theoretically offers a more accurate inflation index.

While this change could help relieve some of the financial pressures on Social Security, it’s an adjustment that would be felt most keenly by current beneficiaries. Imagining Nana and Pop-Pop having to subsist on ramen and tuna fish because of this change makes it a difficult adjustment to sell to the American public.

Change and compromise

It’s likely that we’ll see a combination of tweaks to our system to avert the Social Security shortfall. Raising (or eliminating) the taxable maximum and encouraging immigration, especially among higher-income immigrants, are two of the solutions that seem most likely to quickly move the needle as we decide how to handle our increased life expectancy.

Our politicians are afraid to touch Social Security’s imminent shortfall for good reason: There’s no silver bullet that will solve the problem. Each potential solution must balance the financial, political, and social costs. Understanding how these possible solutions could work can help us start the arduous process of proposing and implementing them.

#10240. Google launches Intelligent Eyewear glasses: $395+, pre-order today, ships Dec. 10

After years of development, Google is launching its second foray into smart glasses with Intelligent Eyewear that supports Android and iOS. Pre-orders start today at Gentle Monster and Warby Parker, with the audio glasses shipping on December 10.

Hands-on: Google and Samsung’s vision for Android XR glasses is 20/20

Intelligent Eyewear is meant to be worn all day rather than the sunglasses-heavy approach taken by others. The frames are 40-44 grams with the weight balanced evenly.

There is a 12-megapixel ultra-wide camera for photos and videos (3K 30FPS or 1080p). You get image stabilization and HDR processing, while four microphones work to provide spatial audio capture. Google is also quite proud of its noise cancellation work.

There are two open-ear speakers for balanced audio and clear vocals. Control is done by a touchpad that accepts taps and swipes, or via voice commands, with Google debuting a new “Hey Gemini” hotword.

Another way to control Intelligent Eyewear is through your Pixel Watch or Galaxy Watch, with Fitbit Air support coming next year:

Notably, Gemini commands that invoke the camera — like visual search or translation — will not save images or videos to your Gemini History. These visuals won’t be used to train AI models or for ad targeting. Additionally, the glasses will “automatically redact bystanders’ faces from these visuals before Gemini processes them.”

Battery life (245mAh) is rated at nine hours on a single charge, with a fully topped-up charging case (Gentle Monster’s shown below) offering seven full charges. Power is transferred via contact pins located on the underside of the nose bridge.

Android XR runs on the Qualcomm Snapdragon AR1 Gen 1 with 2GB of RAM and 64GB of storage. Other specifications include Bluetooth 5.4, Wi-Fi 6E, and IPX4 water resistance. Samsung is responsible for engineering the hardware, while there are two eyewear brands at launch.

Warby Parker Intelligent Eyewear is available in three styles and a total of 14 variations. Alden, Reid, and Wren are inspired by the brand’s “most beloved silhouettes.” Pricing starts at $395 for optical and sun styles in Pine, Saddle, and Jet Black.

The Gentle Monster Intelligent Eyewear collection features six frames in bold colors like dark red, pink, gray, and yellow, with 16 total variations. They can be paired with tinted, clear, blue, or brown lenses, with prescription options available for most designs. Pricing starts at $449 and will be available in the US and South Korea.

Intelligent Eyewear can be used for contextual visual searches, asking Gemini about your day, and having it accomplish tasks.

Google Maps offers turn-by-turn directions, while there’s real-time Google Translate in over 70 languages.

Like on phones, Gemini Guided Vision “offers conversational audio descriptions to people with vision impairments.” This can be used to read fine print, identify color differences, find items, and explore unfamiliar places.

These glasses also serve as always-available headphones with support for YouTube Music, Spotify, Apple Music, and Audible. The Glasses companion app supports:
