#10239. 5 Best AI Anime Video Generators in 2026, and Are AI Anime Videos Worth Making?

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

AI video generators can now turn a prompt or a character image into a few seconds of animation, and anime is one of the most popular styles people ask for. But anime is also one of the hardest styles to get right: flat colors, thin linework and stylized motion expose the weaknesses of video models quickly. For developers and designers, the useful question is not which tool is “best”, but what each one actually offers, what it cannot do yet, and how to fit it into a real production workflow.

This article compares five generators on what their own pages state, covers the problems they all share, asks whether AI anime videos are worth making, and then explains how the models work and how designers and developers can build a practical workflow, including ffmpeg and API-integration examples. “Best” here depends on the job: the tools are listed in no ranking order, each is linked once to its official site for reference, and the comparison is based on public vendor pages reviewed in November 2026. Features, models and pricing change often, so verify current details before relying on any of them.

We reviewed each vendor’s own site and compared what it states on the same points. This is a documentation-based comparison, not a lab benchmark. Where a page does not state something, we say so instead of guessing.

AI anime video generator by Pollo AI sits within a general AI video platform. On its main site, Pollo describes generating video from text prompts or uploaded images and editing existing videos, such as adding, changing, removing or restyling content. It also offers AI image generation, so a character image and the animation can be made in one place.

Strengths for anime work: text-to-video and image-to-video in the same tool, plus video editing and restyling, which suits experimenting with looks.

Limitations and gaps: the pages we could read do not name the underlying models, list credit amounts or pricing, or describe anime-specific controls such as reference characters or first and last frame inputs. You will need to test consistency yourself.

Fits: creators who want image, video and editing tools in one platform and are comfortable testing results before committing.

Vidu lists text-to-video, image-to-video and reference-to-video modes. For image-to-video you can set first and last frames. Reference-to-video lets you upload several images of a character, object or scene, and saved references can be reused through a My References feature. The site highlights 2D animation and diverse artistic styles, mentions 1080p output and offers an API platform aimed at enterprise use.

Strengths for anime work: the clearest set of consistency tools among the five pages we reviewed, with first and last frames, multi-image references and reusable saved characters.

Limitations and gaps: the page does not specify clip durations beyond examples, detail its anime-specific templates, or list prices. Free credits are mentioned without an amount.

Fits: sequences built around a recurring character, and teams that want an API.

Kling AI presents Kling 4.0 for video, described as offering stable dynamic motion and an audio-visual experience, alongside an image model, a Motion Control tool and a node-based Canvas editor for working through scripts, storyboards, images and video. It also lists MCP and CLI support for batch generation and automated production, and an API platform with documentation.

Strengths for anime work: motion-focused tooling and a workflow environment for storyboards and multi-step production, plus automation options for developers.

Limitations and gaps: the page we reviewed does not detail image-to-video specifics, first and last frame controls, camera control, durations, video resolution or pricing, and it gives no anime-specific guidance.

Fits: teams that value motion control and scripted or batch pipelines.

Hailuo AI, from MiniMax, describes creating AI videos and images from text or photos. Its page shows a reference field and an Omni Reference option, a banner for a model that mentions multimodal generation and editing, and many photo-based templates such as photo-to-motion, transformation and style transfer.

Strengths for anime work: an accessible, template-driven way to animate a still image and try stylized effects quickly.

Limitations and gaps: the page does not explain how reference works, or state camera control, durations, resolution, API availability or pricing. Template-driven results may be harder to control precisely than prompt- and frame-driven workflows.

Fits: quick experiments and social clips made from a single image.

Dreamina describes itself as an all-in-one creative platform for images, videos and talking avatars. For video it lists text-to-video, image-to-video, sketch-to-video, cartoon video generation and reference-to-video, using several Seedance models, along with editing examples such as green-screen replacement. It also offers image generation and upscaling.

Strengths for anime work: a broad toolset, including cartoon-oriented generation, references and editing in one environment.

Limitations and gaps: no official maximum duration or video resolution is stated, and the page notes that displayed pricing is for reference only and that final pricing requires signing in. The breadth of features and models can make it harder to know which one to use for a given shot.

Fits: creators who want images, video and avatars under one roof.

“Not stated” means the vendor page we reviewed did not say, not that the feature does not exist. Treat the table as a checklist of questions to answer in your own tests.

It depends on the job and on what you compare them with. Against a full studio production they are limited. Against having no animation at all, they change what a small team or solo creator can attempt.

Treat the generator as a fast prototyping and shot-making assistant, not a replacement for writing, direction and design. Audience reaction also varies, and some viewers are openly critical of AI-made work, so quality and disclosure both matter.

Most current generators are diffusion models extended to video. As in image diffusion, the model starts from random noise and removes it step by step, guided by your inputs. The extension to video, described in research such as Video Diffusion Models, is that the model denoises a whole sequence of frames together, so that motion and appearance stay coherent over time. Many systems work in a compressed latent space rather than on raw pixels to keep generation affordable.

Create an original character sheet with front, side and three-quarter views, a fixed color palette and a clear silhouette. Keep it simple: fewer fine details means less flicker.

Break the sequence into short shots with one action and one camera move each. A four-shot, twenty-second sequence is more realistic than one long generation.

Start each shot from a clean keyframe of your character. Where a tool supports first and last frames or reference images, use them to define the pose and keep identity stable.

Describe subject, action, camera and mood, and add a style anchor. For example: “The girl slowly turns toward the camera, wind moves her hair, petals drift past, gentle push-in, 2D cel shading, clean linework.”

Scrub through each clip for warped hands, drifting faces and flickering lines. Discard or regenerate failures instead of hoping nobody notices.

Join the best takes, color-match them, add sound and captions, and add disclosure where a platform requires it.

Developers can make the pipeline repeatable. Two patterns help: scripted post-processing with ffmpeg, and a resilient job-based client for any generation API.

The script below extracts a last frame to seed the next shot, normalizes clips to a common size and frame rate so they can be joined, concatenates them, and optionally holds each frame twice for an “on twos” look. Adjust sizes and frame rates to your project.

Video generation is usually asynchronous: you submit a job, then poll or receive a callback. The sketch below shows the pattern with a timeout and backoff. The endpoints and fields are placeholders, so follow your provider’s documentation for real ones.

Most are diffusion models for video. They start from noise and remove it step by step across a sequence of frames, guided by a text prompt and often a starting image or reference images, until coherent motion appears.

Usually, for consistency. The image locks the character and style, while the prompt only needs to describe motion.

Thin lines and flat color regions make small frame-to-frame changes visible. Simpler designs, slower motion and post-processing reduce it.

Partly. Reference images, saved characters and shared keyframes help, but you should still review every shot for drift.

For short clips, concept previews and storyboards, often yes. For long, dialogue-driven stories, not yet.

It depends on the tool and plan. Read the current terms and make sure you have rights to any characters or assets you upload.

Run the same character image and prompt through each, then compare consistency, line stability, motion quality and cost per usable second.

AI anime video generators are useful, but uneven. The five tools reviewed here differ in input modes, consistency tools, developer access and how much their own pages say, and none removes the core problems of consistency, flicker and limited acting. The practical approach is to test several tools on the same shots, keep your workflow tool-agnostic, design characters that are simple and consistent, and review every clip before it ships. Used that way, they are a capable prototyping and shot-making aid, not a substitute for design and direction.

#10236. Taxing billionaires failed in California, but other states are taking steps to collect from the rich

State efforts to tax the rich did relatively well in the 2026 midterm elections, following a series of state legislative moves in that direction in recent years.

That might come as a surprise because a majority of voters rejected California’s Proposition 40. The much-publicized ballot initiative would have imposed a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of the state’s roughly 200 billionaires. Google cofounder Sergey Brin and several other billionaires spent nearly $400 million trying to persuade voters to reject it.

Emmanuel Saez, a University of California, Berkeley, economist who studies inequality and helped design Proposition 40, lamented the loss, saying: “Today oligarchy has won.”

As a law professor who recently wrote a book about wealth inequality, I have been monitoring the results of these efforts aimed at taxing the rich. Despite Proposition 40’s failure, I think it’s important to observe that many Americans expressed support during the midterms for hiking income taxes on the rich, and to a lesser extent, taxes on the second—or third or fourth—homes the very wealthy possess.

Taxing the rich at the ballot box

Taxing income is proving a more successful strategy than taxing wealth.

Major changes to income taxes were up for a vote in five states during the midterms. Three of those ballot initiatives were proposals that sought to boost income tax rates on the rich or maintain those rates. All three prevailed.

In Washington state, for example, voters backed a measure that will preserve its new 9.9% income tax on household income above $1 million. This “millionaire’s tax,” signed into law earlier in 2026, is the state’s first personal income tax.

Meanwhile, Colorado voters rejected Proposition 136, which would have capped the state’s income tax rate at 4.4%. They also approved Amendment 87, a new graduated income tax that raises rates on households and businesses with incomes over $500,000.

And even though California’s voters rejected Proposition 40, they did approve Proposition 3. That measure makes permanent the income tax rates enacted in 2012 for the state’s highest earners, which were set to expire in 2031. The surcharges, adjusted annually for inflation, start at 10.3% for incomes of $360,000 and go up to a 12.3% surcharge for taxpayers earning over $721,000.

And in August 2026, Missouri voters overwhelmingly rejected a measure that would have required the state’s lawmakers to eliminate its income tax. This would have meant losing $8.5 billion in revenue annually. The change would have let rich income taxpayers off the hook and replaced lost revenue through an increased sales tax that would have hit low-income taxpayers hardest.

The two losses were in North Carolina and Iowa. Neither state voted directly on a tax to be levied on the rich. But both approved constitutional amendments that will make it harder for the state legislatures to enact these kinds of taxes in the future. North Carolina’s governor, Josh Stein, called the amendment in his state a “millionaire protection cap.”

State legislatures raising income tax rates on high earners

Ahead of the midterms, new taxes on the rich introduced via state legislatures, rather than ballot initiatives, also emerged.

In Maine, legislators voted in April 2026 for a tax surcharge of 1% on income over $1 million. The following month, Hawaiian lawmakers created a new 13% income bracket for single taxpayers earning above $500,000 or couples filing jointly who make over $1 million. This change is paired with a reduction in rates for lower-income brackets.

And one month after that, Rhode Island enacted a surcharge for millionaires’ income to be phased in over the next three years, reaching a maximum 3% rate.

In 2009, New York became one of the first states to pass one of these high-earner income taxes. Washington, D.C., Massachusetts, and Maryland also enacted these “millionaire taxes” in 2022, 2023, and 2025, respectively.

Taxing additional homes

Another way that state and local governments are boosting the tax revenue they get from wealthy constituents is by levying special taxes on pricey homes that aren’t the owners’ primary residences. These initiatives have succeeded both in state legislatures and voting booths.

Montana lawmakers, in April 2025, approved a new tiered property tax system, which took effect on January 1, 2026. It raised property tax rates on vacation homes and short-term rentals to 1.9%, while primary residences and qualifying long-term rentals pay lower, tiered homestead rates.

New York City rolled out its “pied-à-terre tax” in July. The new tax imposes an annual surcharge of 0.8% to 1.3% on single-family homes valued at $5 million or more, and 4% to 6.5% on condos and co-ops valued at $1 million or more. The surcharge only applies to homes that are not a primary residence.

Rhode Island has a similar property tax that took effect at the same time as New York City’s. It’s an annual surcharge of $2.50 for every $500 of assessed value above $1 million that applies to non-primary residences.

And on November 3, voters in Boulder, Colorado, approved a residential vacancy tax on homes that sit empty more than half the year. The surcharge, which goes into effect in 2028, will be roughly $4,000 a year for each vacant property. It applies across the board, but homes that aren’t primary residences are the clear target.

However, just west of Boulder in Crested Butte, Colorado, a second-home tax failed. So did an effort to levy a similar surcharge in San Diego, California.

Why income taxes are attractive to voters and lawmakers

There is a good reason why taxing the income of rich people is easier to pull off than taxing their wealth: Income taxes are much easier to calculate.

Income taxes can be based on annual income tax filings, whether state or federal. It requires no extra work to value someone’s net worth. There are no such filings for wealth, except after death, if a large estate is left behind.

Wealth taxes also require the annual valuation of businesses, farmland, artwork, intellectual property, and other assets—many of which are hard to estimate.

The downside of taxing income instead of wealth is that it limits how much revenue can be raised from the people most able to pay taxes. Most wealthy people convert little of their wealth into income. One common exception occurs when they sell some of their stock.

Property taxes, like income taxes, are an exception to this rule. Calculating how much tax on real estate someone owes is easy for the authorities to do using annual municipal assessments.

What might happen next?

Despite Proposition 40’s defeat, it looks like Americans are generally open to taxing wealthy people more—at least when the states do it.

In Illinois, where a billionaire governor, JB Pritzker, easily won a third term, another interesting ballot initiative prevailed.

More than 75% of voters in Cook County, which includes Chicago and several of its suburbs, approved a nonbinding, advisory referendum asking if Illinois should adopt the “millionaire amendment for property tax relief and education.” It would levy a new surcharge of 3% on incomes over $1 million. While this win did not authorize a new tax, it revealed that support for one would be strong—at least in Chicago and Evanston.

Even billionaire Bill Gates has said he believes a “billionaire’s tax” will be necessary. The question is: What kind?

Allison Anna Tait is a professor of law at the University of Richmond.

#10235. 5 ways to turn your cold outreach into a job offer

Taylor Stanton, a former student of mine, spent nearly 15 years as a communications professional for tech CEOs in Silicon Valley. On the side, he photographed the underexplored backcountry of national parks and posted the images with educational content on social media, drawing around 20 million impressions. When he turned that work into a self-published book, he doubled his investment within 48 hours of launch. That same year, he landed a job with the largest congressionally chartered foundation supporting public lands, an opportunity he says came from his thought leadership about those underexplored places. Turns out, his work had been making the introduction for months.

Most job seekers try to make that introduction in one cold message, and the odds are against them. In an analysis of 12 million outreach emails, only 8.5% got a reply. Leading with an elevator pitch, which many critics have now declared dead, makes it worse because it’s about the speaker, or writer, rather than the listener.

When a marketing message flops, I look at the customer before I touch the copy. In a job search, the customer is the hiring manager who needs someone to solve a problem. So instead of a pitch, ask an Elevator Question, a surprising question that shows how you think about someone else’s problem in an uncommon way and introduces a possibility the company may not have considered. Here’s how.

1. Find the problem everyone else overlooks, and the person who owns it

Pick a company you’d genuinely like to join. Read its announcements, leadership interviews, and industry coverage. Find a challenge connected to your target role, then ask yourself what the coverage is missing that you see clearly.

Let’s say a growing consumer packaged goods brand is investing the majority of its budget on customer acquisition. A common question might be whether awareness or conversion is the bigger challenge. A distinctive question might sound like, “As you attract new shoppers, how do you reengage the ones who show interest but aren’t ready to buy?” The distinctive question allows the candidate to signal expertise in a commonly underfunded stage of the direct-to-consumer funnel. You don’t need years of experience to do this. Public information and analysis are enough to show critical thinking, a skill that’s increasingly sought after in the AI era.

Finally, be sure to send the message to the person who owns that problem, usually the hiring manager or their boss, not the CEO or recruiter. You don’t need years of experience.

2. Publish the evidence before you hit send

Hiring managers will likely look you up online. In a CareerBuilder survey of more than 1,000 hiring managers, 70% said they research on social media, and 47% said they’re less likely to interview someone they can’t find online. So clean up your profiles, then fill them with your original ideas.

Publish one short teaching post a week on LinkedIn. This structure works well:

A relatable, story-based opening. “We thought our retargeting was optimized until our KPIs declined for three straight ad cycles. Consumers didn’t mind a reminder but they did mind reminders they’d learned to tune out.”

A surprising segue. “Retargeting isn’t dead. Most of us just run it in the way we did 10 years ago. A funnel based on video play time is the new way to decide who gets reminders, without them feeling like reminders.”

A framework. Teach three to five steps readers can take to implement a better way, and name it.

When you have time, to this weekly routine you can add a simple personal website with a short bio, a newsletter signup, and your posts in a blog section. As artificial intelligence summaries replace search results, a personal website that you control helps shape what the internet says about you.

3. Let them see you

Under the 90-9-1 rule, 90% of online users mostly watch, 9% contribute occasionally, and 1% create most of the content. Posting consistently sets you apart, and video sets you apart even more. Prop your phone on some books and spend 30 to 60 seconds explaining that week’s idea. I call this the FaceTime Effect. People trust you more when they feel they’ve met you, and an imperfect video does that better than a list of boring credentials that can be found elsewhere, like on social bios or that personal website I mentioned.

Share the post on Instagram, too. In a Zety survey reported by SHRM, 76% of Gen Z respondents said they use Instagram for career content and networking, compared with 34% for LinkedIn, a shift that FastCompany has covered. In general, repetition helps. Under the mere exposure effect, the more often we encounter something, the more we tend to like it.

4. Lead with a question, not a résumé summary

Now write the message. Send it by email if you can find a verified address. Otherwise send it on LinkedIn. In the same outreach study, personalized subject lines lifted responses by 30.5%.

Subject: Your growth strategy

Hi [Name],

As you grow conversions, how do you reengage people who show interest but aren’t ready to buy? I’ve been following [Company]’s expansion and keep coming back to the consideration phase of the customer journey because it’s so cost-effective compared to the awareness phase.

I explored that question in a short LinkedIn post [Link].

I hope it’s helpful,

[Your Name]

There’s purposefully no request for a meeting. When you give something useful first, everyone knows a reply becomes the natural next step.

5. Follow up once, then widen your reach

Silence could mean rejection but it could also mean a busy week or the wrong inbox. After five to seven business days, send one sentence asking whether they saw your note. In the outreach study, one follow-up increased replies by 65.8%. Resist adding more, though. Someone who doesn’t engage today may need you in a few months, so you want to be remembered as helpful, not desperate or annoying.

Then find a second contact, such as an alum or mutual connection. They don’t need to be close to you. A LinkedIn study of 20 million users, published in Science, found that moderately weak ties, defined as people with whom you share about 10 mutual connections, were the most useful for landing new jobs. Mention your earlier note without asking them to chase it: “In case I reached the wrong person, I wanted to share this with you, too.”

6. Make your thinking the reason they reach out

Taylor Stanton’s photos circulated for a long time before his dream job came along. A cold message is one touchpoint. Helpful information, published consistently, keeps working until the right people find you first. That’s the pull marketing effect in action.

An elevator pitch tells someone what you’ve accomplished. An Elevator Question gives them a reason to discuss what you could accomplish together.

#10233. Hands-on: Google and Samsung’s vision for Android XR glasses is 20/20

While I acknowledge Meta’s role in bringing smart glasses to a mainstream audience, it has proven to be an irresponsible steward. Its “growth at all costs” mindset has actively poisoned people’s perception of the form factor. Under Meta’s watch, glasses have gained a creepy connotation before their utility has been fully realized.

Google’s second take on smart glasses is the exact opposite of what Meta has done. Every single aspect has been considered, and the result is worthy of being most people’s introduction to the form factor.

Officially, Android XR glasses are known as Gentle Monster and Warby Parker Intelligent Eyewear. The branding is a mouthful, and I’m not quite sure “Intelligent Eyewear” will take off. Something more colloquial, like “Google glasses” — glasses.google is the landing page — or “Samsung glasses,” will probably stick in the public consciousness.

That critique aside, the name reflects how Google wants Intelligent Eyewear to actually replace your existing glasses. Unlike the Ray-Ban trap that I frankly think Meta did not consider, Google’s offerings are not situational or activity-based devices like sunglasses. These are a “smart” upgrade to the assistive device some people have to wear.

As a wearable, smart glasses are a bit like smartwatches in that the platonic design is pretty well established and indistinguishable from traditional eyewear. Unlike watches, glasses are so visible on people’s faces that form overrides everything else.

Fortunately, the Samsung hardware I wore for an hour last week looks and feels like glasses, almost unremarkably so. I’d venture to say that audio-only glasses without a display are a solved design challenge. Google emphasized that, at 41 grams, this is the lightest pair of smart glasses on the market, and it worked to make sure the weight is distributed evenly.

The sides of the stems that face your head feature translucent plastic that lets you see the internal components. I liked that small design choice. You can control the glasses using voice commands, with Google debuting a new “Hey Gemini” hotword for the form factor. While “Hey Google” and “OK Google” remain available, the new one is meant to reflect how big a role Gemini plays on smart glasses.

There is also a touchpad on the right stem that accepts taps and swipes, while a button up top lets you take pictures and record video. Another way you’ll be able to control the glasses is with your Pixel Watch and Galaxy Watch. You can play/pause audio and enable Gemini using double-pinch and wrist gestures. Notably, gesture support is also coming to the Fitbit Air next year.

From its internal testing, Google tells me that which input method people use is pretty situational and ends up being natural. At the beginning of my demo, I favored the touchpad, but by the end, I was leaning toward voice commands.

Talking to Intelligent Eyewear uses Gemini Live. Some prompts, like take a picture or play a song, are one-shot “chat” commands in phone parlance, but for the most part, you’re using Gemini’s back-and-forth conversation mode. Google heavily customized the Gemini Live model for glasses to reduce latency, shorten responses, and tightly integrate the camera.

Even compared to my last demo in May, the latency of voice commands has come a long way. That said, I need more time to see if it’s really fast enough to use as a primary interaction method for most commands.

Similarly, Google will blur all faces and filter out bystander voices before it gets uploaded to Gemini in the cloud. This on-device processing occurs on your phone.

Since that visual media isn’t being saved, the external indicator light won’t be active when you’re talking to Gemini. The LED is only on when photos or videos are being saved and can be reviewed later.

That indicator light features anti-tamper detection that prevents recording. Algorithms detect whether the LED is covered by stickers or markers, with this process featuring hardware verification when the glasses are in their charging case.

Google’s “Glasses” companion app, with Samsung having a near-identical version for Galaxy phones, is pretty similar to the version for Pixel Watch. Unlike the bloated “Meta AI” app, it’s just for settings rather than the very definition of a growth hack with a full chatbot. The difference is staggering, and something Google deserves a bit of credit for in this age of throwing AI into every crevice of day-to-day smartphone usage.

Under the hood, the glasses are offloading a lot of processing to your phone. This includes HDR pipelines and video stabilization. The 12MP camera takes pictures in a 4:3 aspect ratio, while you can record up to 90 seconds of video. Images are transferred immediately to your phone over Wi-Fi, while videos wait until the glasses are charging to preserve battery life. I am so excited by point-of-view photography and the instantaneous capture the glasses offer, and early impressions of camera quality are positive.

Another thing I want to test is how Intelligent Eyewear fares as always-available headphones. There are two open-ear speakers and four microphones, and Google is clearly very proud of the noise-cancellation work in place.

As someone who has been waiting for smart glasses since 2012, I cannot overstate my annoyance at how Meta allowed smart glasses to gain a scummy undertone, if not overtone. It should have been more proactive to societal issues. Meanwhile, Meta releasing glasses without a camera, thus removing the primary utility of real-world context, makes me deeply question its belief that this is the future.

Smart glasses that know what you’re interacting with in the world can be extremely useful. That always-available camera is a genuine physical advantage over smartphones. It unlocks new use cases and convenience that are just not possible with something that goes in your pocket.

Google took a long time to get back to glasses. From what I’ve used so far, the wait will be worth it. The hardware and designs are solid, while the software is chock-full of innovative, well-considered ideas.

The Government Accountability Office says record-keeping, inventory monitoring, and staff training need to be improved.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Pentagon is struggling to track an astonishing 26 million F-35 warfighter parts, worth an estimated $31 billion, according to analysis published by the Government Accountability Office (GAO) this week. In its report — published just weeks after China purportedly swiped a classified shipment of F-35 parts diverted through Hong Kong — the GAO criticized the current inventory system as “outdated, inaccurate, and incomplete.” Possible solutions were also provided by the GAO; however, the implications are that the most advanced and costly fighter jets in U.S. history may not be ready and reliable due to inventory management deficiencies.

Inventory problems have been a long-standing feature of the deployment of the F-35, notes the source. The F-35 program is estimated to cost $1.9 trillion over its lifecycle. It is the most costly weapon system in history, says the GAO. But the Department of Defense (DOD) has “long-standing and ongoing deficiencies related to the accountability and financial reporting of F-35 parts,” asserts the watchdog.

Chief among the issues that need to be addressed is the headlining massive unmonitored pool of roughly 26 million spare parts. These are spread among 700 government and contractor facilities worldwide, but the technology for managing massive inventories has existed for decades.

We might have seen a telling symptom of the inadequate F-35 parts tracking system back in September. A communications and/or accountability breakdown resulted in a UPS worker routing top-secret parts through Hong Kong to save time. They were allegedly swiped by China after an employee is thought to have missed an email warning not to divert the parts.

Frustratingly, this is the third report since 2019 from the GAO, and the latest published report complains that the DOD has “made minimal progress” in implementing past recommendations. For example, in a 2022 report, periodic physical inventories of F-35 parts were recommended but have not been implemented yet, notes Stars and Stripes. There is also no reliable procedure for verifying data from prime contractors, which can be “inaccurate and incomplete.”

Currently, it is believed that there are over 1 million parts, worth more than $85 million, that are lost or missing. Moreover, about 17,000 parts that have been sent in for repair, worth as much as $42.5 billion, aren’t tracked.

Stars and Stripes mentions that the Pentagon is working on “a live connection” for the F-35 Joint Program Office (JPO), bridging its inventory software and that of prime contractors with F-35 parts. The JPO asserts that it is now modernizing its infrastructure with direct real-time interfaces. “This integration directly addresses previous system gaps to ensure seamless accountability of F-35 spare parts,” said a JPO spokesperson, quoted by Breaking Defense.

#10231. A cyberattack forces you to pull the plug. Can your business keep running?

The recent cyberattack on European supermarkets sent the temperature in some Swedish freezers to a sweltering 131 F (55 C). The Dutch grocery chain Ahold Delhaize warned that a separate hack could strip up to 250 million euros ($277 million) from sales, and wipe as much as 100 million euros off operating profit in the fourth quarter. 

This recent spate of cyberattacks around the world, including a staggering $6.3 billion heist at the crypto exchange Binance, lays bare a blind spot in many boardrooms. Directors too often ask whether attackers can break into their systems. They should also be asking whether the business can take the hit and keep running.

Boards should assume attackers will get through. It’s a question of when, not if. And when they do, can the business still fulfill orders, pay staff, and keep critical facilities open? 

Too rare

Unfortunately, this is often not the case in the companies that I deal with. I recently worked with a board that had rightly grown more worried about cyber threats, and drafted in a former spy to carry out a cyber audit. The contractor ran penetration tests, hacked a few of the firm’s products, and found holes in its defenses. 

That’s fairly typical. The audit tested whether hackers could penetrate the company’s defenses. But it stopped short of testing whether the business could ride out a breach. And this is the gap I see running through many companies. 

Sometimes, stopping an attack from spreading means shutting down the very systems that keep you operating. 

Ahold Delhaize took some of its own websites and apps down as a precaution after the cyberattack, cutting off online shopping for some customers. The Dutch group contained most of the disruption within two weeks and it was getting back to normal once it reported third-quarter results. In Belgium, it had online shopping back up and running just a week after disclosing the breach. 

Contrast that with Marks & Spencer, the British retail stalwart. After a breach in April 2025, it stopped taking online clothing orders for a spell of 46 days. And when orders finally resumed, only part of its clothing range was available.

If you have to pull the plug on your own systems to contain a breach, how will you keep serving customers? 

The AI factor

AI is only raising the stakes. It’s my view that cyber threats have changed more in the past six months than in the previous six years. But many companies haven’t caught up.

Some of the newest crop of AI models are spotting security flaws that their predecessors missed, and have worked out how to exploit some of them. 

Take Anthropic’s Mythos Preview, which scored about 83% on a cybersecurity benchmark, compared with roughly 67% for the company’s previous best model, Claude Opus 4.6. Anthropic says it spotted thousands of security flaws, many of them serious, including in every major operating system and web browser. Worrying indeed. 

Last week, OpenAI released GPT‑6 Cyber to vetted customers. The model is designed to find security flaws and test whether they can be exploited.

The U.K.’s National Cyber Security Centre says the gap between a flaw becoming public and attackers exploiting it has already shrunk to just days. And it predicts that AI will compress that window further still, giving defenders even less time to patch the holes.

The most recent spate of supermarket hacks came on the heels of a similar hack of fridges at hundreds of French supermarkets. The result was piles of spoiled food, and fires even broke out.

Following that breach, Danfoss, the Danish industrial company that made the temperature controls, urged its customers to update their software and hardware. But just weeks later, hackers hit retailers using Danfoss controls again. This time, stores in several European countries were hit, including Sweden and Ireland.

Some fared better than others. Carrefour said it had installed updates and secured its connections after the first wave of attacks, steps it credited with curbing the numbers of its Belgian stores hit. Acting on the first warning helped Carrefour blunt the next attack.

Some retailers left their refrigeration systems exposed. That’s unacceptable. But even with tighter security, you still need a way to trade when the systems you depend on go dark.

What to do

Protect the operations you can least afford to lose. Then drill your teams on how to keep them running through an attack. When the malware designated NotPetya hit Maersk in 2017, the shipping giant handled about 80% of its usual volume manually. Staff taped paperwork to containers and took orders through personal Gmail accounts.

Consider a distribution center that needs to keep essential goods moving. Ask one team to fulfill a handful of priority orders without its usual order system or company email. Can staff confirm orders using a secure offline list and an agreed backup channel, check stock by hand and arrange transport? Have them log each dispatch on paper and check those logs against the order system once it’s back online.

When the drill ends, ask how much of the usual workload the team handled safely, for how long, and where it got stuck. Give each fix an owner and a deadline, then run the drill again.

Find out how long you can keep serving customers with your systems down. A real attack is a brutal way to get the answer.

#10229. The FAA’s IT troubles are far bigger then AI

U.S. airlines are still reeling from a nationwide ground stop issued on Friday that interrupted weekend travel and wreaked havoc on schedules. The culprit, the Federal Aviation Administration says, was simply outdated tech.

The ground stop was followed by eager speculation on social media about what might have caused the issue. Some pointed a finger at a new AI system that the FAA integrated earlier in the week; others blamed foreign adversaries. At the same time, a range of tech companies that contract with the FAA, like Microsoft,were quick to distance themselves from the agency’s problems. 

Later Friday evening, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told reporters the outage occurred after an old analog system called time-division multiplexing became overloaded. This is an arcane system of processing data signals over a network. The overload, in turn, impacted the telecommunications systems used by terminal radar approach controls, or TRACONs, the air traffic control facilities that help direct flights at airports. Duffy noted that systems that had already been upgraded based on internet protocols did not experience the outage. “This is all the old legacy equipment,” he said. “All of the new equipment that’s been deployed did not go down.”

Officials, at least for now, insist there’s no evidence anything nefarious happened. Instead, the Department of Transportation is, once again, begging Congress for more money to overhaul FAA tech. 

Duffy urged Congress to provide additional funding to modernize the nation’s air traffic control system, arguing that the issue should transcend partisan politics. He noted that the FAA had received $15 billion for modernization efforts over the past 25 years, with little to show for it. “It’s not red, it’s not blue, it’s not Democrat, it’s not Republican, it’s American,” he told reporters. “Give us the money to fix it.”

Indeed, the FAA’s tech problems are way bigger than AI. Instead, they have a lot more to do with the challenges of updating technology while it’s being used. 

The pilots guidance system is ancient and isn’t designed to handle upgrades

This isn’t the first time the FAA has experienced a major outage that’s brought flights across the country to a halt. Back in 2023, the Notice to Airmen system (NOTAM), which alerts pilots to potential hazards in American airspace, went offline after contractors accidentally deleted files, disrupting its core technology.

There’s been an effort to improve the NOTAM system, but it’s moving at a snail’s pace. The FAA has brought in private industry for help and engaged in an effort to modernize the system, but that process has only brought to light myriad other problems. For one, at least according to contract paperwork obtained last year, NOTAMs weren’t exclusively being stored in a virtual environment or in an entirely digital format. Another aspiration the FAA was working on, at least at the time: making sure that upgrades to some systems didn’t disrupt, well, all of air traffic control.

“Everyone will say, ‘Well, there’s backups in place,’” Shawn Pruchnicki, a former pilot who is a professor at Ohio State University’s Department of Aviation, told FedScoop at the time. “But we’ve also seen time and time again where those things have been said and things have gone horribly wrong.”

Poor AI rollout

Like a lot of other federal agencies, the Federal Aviation Administration has been inching toward deploying artificial intelligence for a host of applications. Back in 2023, the Department of Transportation, of which the FAA is part, said ChatGPT was being used for certain purposes, which the FAA said at the time was incorrect. Since then, though, the FAA has begun to embrace AI: An inventory of use cases released by the government references several uses, including AI-powered pilot voice transcription, systems for detecting drones, and meteorology.

But the FAA hasn’t been the best at communicating to the public how it plans to use AI safely, without becoming susceptible to the risks of the technology. 

Many people, early on, suspected that Friday’s outage might have been related to the SMART system, an AI-based airspace planning tool the agency introduced earlier in the week. The FAA explains that the tool is designed to “analyze airline schedules, weather, airport capacity, airspace conditions, and operational constraints to predict traffic flows and identify potential conflicts before they occur.” SMART doesn’t appear to have had anything to do with the ground stop, though. 

Bad wires and old hardware

The deficiency of the FAA’s timeworn infrastructure was on display in April 2025, when a burned copper wire triggered a communications blackout at Newark Liberty International Airport. For 90 seconds, air traffic controllers lost radar and radio contact with planes approaching one of the nation’s busiest airports. The incident triggered weeks of delays and cancellations. Another communications failure followed in May. 

Newark’s hiccup was the sign of an endemic problem: Some of the FAA’s copper wiring dates back to the 1960s, and according to a September 2026 report from the Government Accountability Office (GAO), the FAA had replaced fewer than half of its aging copper wires, 2,560 out of 5,170.

And it’s not just wires. Back in 2007, the FAA began a technological overhaul known as NextGen, which aimed to reduce its reliance on ground-based radar in favor of satellite navigation and digital communications. Nearly two decades later, that effort remains unfinished, due in part to years of inadequate funding. Just earlier this month, the FAA proudly announced it had finally begun retiring floppy disks.

“What we’re doing is hard and it hasn’t happened in the past because it is hard. But I’ll tell you by doing nothing, you inject way more risk into the system,” Duffy said on Friday. “To use 1980s technology, 1990s software . . . 1970s radar that we don’t even make parts for anymore, to have an old network configuration from the 1980s versus re-networking the air traffic control system through the FAA, I believe that should be a priority,” he said.

The FAA’s tech is the problem no one wants to fix

Duffy came into office as transportation secretary promising to overhaul the FAA’s aging technology. In May 2025, he unveiled an ambitious plan to rebuild the nation’s air traffic control system by 2028 and replace critical infrastructure like radars and radios. Congress approved an initial $12.5 billion for the effort, but the price tag quickly jumped. Just two months later, Duffy told lawmakers that the full overhaul would cost an estimated $31.5 billion. Even his 2028 deadline comes with an asterisk. It covers only the first phase of modernization, with no timetable yet established for the second, which includes new software to track aircraft and manage air traffic. 

The GAO put it most damningly in its September 2026 report, writing that the FAA “doesn’t have a lifecycle cost estimate or master schedule for related projects,” which “could end up causing air traffic disruptions or prolonging reliance on severely outdated systems.” These tech problems only exacerbate the FAA’s other endemic challenges, including overworked air traffic control offices and a controller recruitment crisis.

Meanwhile, the $30 billion Modern Skies Act, sponsored by Senator Eric Schmitt of Missouri and aiming to fund upgrades on everything from air traffic control software to airport terminals, has yet to advance out of committee. And on November 13, the White House asked Congress for another $30.1 billion for aviation infrastructure, including $10.1 billion for air traffic control technology.

When asked whether Americans could be sure that the issues seen Friday wouldn’t occur again, Duffy was blunt: “I can’t build things if I don’t have money.”

#10228. Here’s how Google’s Android XR glasses are handling the camera & privacy

It’s a shame, because a camera in smart glasses serves such a functional role, both for the user in just capturing pictures and for the AI assistant built into the experience. I recently talked about how the camera was my favorite part of smart glasses in an issue of our 9to5Google Weekender newsletter, but how it just feels a bit wrong now.

Anyway, with that context in mind, let’s look at how Google is handling this touchy subject.

Importantly, the light on each pair of Android XR glasses is also designed to avoid any tampering. Android XR glasses automatically perform a system check to ensure the light is working on a regular basis – you might catch the light blinking in white and blue while charging which is a part of the system check ensuring the hardware is fully functional. If the light is found not to be working, the camera is disabled.

Continuing on with how the camera interacts with Gemini, Google explained in a conversation with 9to5Google that Gemini is tuned not to use the camera in cases where it’s not obvious that the user wants the camera to be active. An interaction such as “what painting is this” would very clearly imply that the user wants the glasses to view the scene in front of them and identify the art piece, where “how much money is on the table,” Google explained, would ask for a follow-up before using the camera seeing as it’s not obvious that the user expects the camera to be used in that sort of phrase.

Another way in which Android XR glasses will avoid the recording stigma is with their limits. Google is limiting Intelligent Eyewear video recording to 90-second sessions. While that does limit what the user can do, Google said that most recordings fell within that window anyway. Meta, by comparison, offers recordings up to 5 minutes.

A contractor faced a project that required them to create 50,000 custom Cat6 cables from scratch, requiring 100,000 Cat6 terminations. The contractor, who goes by Analytical Horsepower on YouTube, had used a large, rare tool to streamline the job, but afterward he decided to build his own portable tool by modifying a Milwaukee Hackzall, cutting the time to straighten the twisted pairs to under two seconds.

His first solution to the problem was to buy a “Wire Straightening Machine” from Alibaba for $500. It does the job well enough, but it’s an industrial machine designed for tabletop use, requiring an AC power source for the power brick and compressed air to run. The concept is that it clamps the wire between two rubber grips using air pressure, and then a linkage converts the rotary motion of the motor into a linear one, allowing the grip to untwist the cable. Since he wanted to use the machine in the field, he needed to make the thing portable — so he disassembled the entire thing, replaced the DC power brick with a 20V DeWalt battery with an adapter, added a push-button switch for power control, and a portable bike pump to deliver compressed air on the go.

It worked well at first, but he soon discovered that it was too bulky to use in the tight and hard-to-reach places where Ethernet cables sometimes terminate, like when you’re installing this heavy-duty outdoor Wi-Fi 7 access point. So, he studied the concept — it involved two flat, grippy surfaces grabbing the twisted cables and then moving back and forth. The back-and-forth motion of the surfaces causes the cables to untwist, with the clamping force ensuring that it remains in contact with the cables as they become flatter.

With this, he realized that he did not need such a bulky machine to do the job — he just needed a reciprocating tool that could accept a clamp. He first looked at a reciprocating saw, but he found that it still had the same bulky problem and also called it “not overly precise.” But when he looked at the Milwaukee Hackzall, he found that it offered the perfect balance of portability and precision. More importantly, it came with a detailed data sheet, instruction manual, and parts breakdown that allowed him to accurately 3D print the plastic parts and laser-cut and bend the metal parts he needed to build his machine. He also used a toggle clamp to hold the Cat6 cable in place instead of a pneumatic piston, which further simplified the machine and cut its size and weight.

After a few steps of trial and error, especially in the quality of the grippy materials used for the clamping surfaces, he finally got it to work. He could reliably untwist softer copper-clad aluminum cables in one go in under two seconds. Harder 100% pure copper conductors, sometimes called solid copper or pure bare copper Ethernet cables, must be untwisted pair-by-pair, though, requiring a bit more time, but it’s still undoubtedly much faster and more convenient than doing the job with just your bare hands.

This tool isn’t worth it if you only untwist a few Ethernet cables every month or so, like this telephone-to-gigabit internet conversion job. But if you’re facing a massive job like Analytical Horsepower, that half a minute you save with every cable end could translate to over 830 cumulative hours of labor saved on the jobsite. It’s a great first-generation tool, with its practical use apparent in the YouTube video. Some commenters suggest extending the toggle clamp handle to reach the trigger so activating the tool is easier, while it also looks like a good idea if there’s a way to incorporate the entire system into a crimper.

#10226. The most important shopper of the future isn’t human

A shopper asks an AI assistant for sneakers for a 23-year-old. Another Googles a boutique hotel in Rome. Before either sees a picture of a shoe or a room, artificial intelligence has helped decide which brands deserve consideration. Mental availability is no longer formed directly by comms and shopper experience; a new intermediary has stepped in.

AI is increasingly a gatekeeper between businesses and their customers. Shoppers don’t have to open a chatbot for AI to influence their choices. It is already embedded in familiar services. Think of Google, where AI-generated answers appear before people visit a brand’s website.

Morgan Stanley estimates that agent-influenced shopping could account for $190 billion to $385 billion in U.S. e-commerce spending by 2030, or 10% to 20% of the market. Of course, being memorable to humans is still essential, but leaders also need to consider whether their brand is understood by AI, not just people.

People can accommodate changing messages within an existing emotional attachment to a brand. Machines do not share that attachment. Fragmented messaging or unsupported claims can leave AI systems with conflicting information, making them less likely to recommend the brand. 

Even the biggest names cannot assume they will appear. Authors writing in Harvard Business Review in 2026 found that Brooks appeared more reliably than Nike in their tests of AI recommendations for running shoes.

The response requires more than trying to influence where AI looks for answers. Brands are racing to SEO, GEO, and Reddit strategies, but the landscape is continually evolving. To remain in consideration by both audiences, brands need to go back to their roots, examine their foundations, and be more disciplined in their execution. They must focus on the core idea the brand stands for and how consistently that meaning comes across wherever the brand appears.

So, how do you do it?

Design your business for humans and machines at the same time

AI does not feel your brand. It can identify the emotions associated with it, but it does not share the attachment that makes someone instinctively reach for your product.

Emotional resonance and machine legibility require a coordinated approach. The question is whether the meaning you have built around your brand is relevant to the shopper. Does it connect to the visual presence you have built, and can the machine validate it all?

Take Dove. Its real beauty message has created a powerful position around inclusion. Yet when we asked an AI assistant to recommend a good cream for sensitive skin, Dove did not appear. Asked why, the assistant associated it with affordability. The brand’s broader message had not translated into relevance to that skincare request.

KitKat has a particularly clear narrative: Take a break. It gives people a reason to reach for the brand beyond simply wanting chocolate, making KitKat come to mind when they want a pause.

Our research into AI and brand magnetism has shown that to build both mental availability and machine awareness, brands need at least three ownable distinctive assets and a clear relevant narrative. To ensure your brand is understood by AI, keep your messaging consistent across channels and over time.

Nike shows that even owning distinctive assets alone is not enough. The Swoosh and “Just Do It” make Nike instantly recognizable, yet when AI was asked to recommend a running shoe for a 23-year-old, it didn’t feature Nike in the top three. Surprising perhaps, but AI points out that competitors have built strong associations with emerging buying needs: New Balance on authenticity, Lululemon with wellness. Not only have other brands created more relevant narratives, Nike’s own is suffering from semantic contradictions: “Just do it,” “Believe in something,” “Why do it?’ Irrespective of how emotional appealing it all is to humans, the machine finds these contradictions and so will not recommend the brand.

Brands structured for this new AI-mediated world have to deal with this new complexity. Build emotional appeal for people alongside information machines can use to understand that relevance. This is the new standard of brand craft, giving creativity a sharper brief. Brands that master both early will be harder to displace.

Build through repetition, coherence, and ownable signals

Once that relevance is established, the brand itself needs to accumulate presence through repeated exposure. The same visual and verbal cues should reinforce one another across websites, retail communications, and social channels.

Research by Charlie Oscar, reported by WARC, analyzed 30 brands across six categories, and attributed 63% of LLM visibility to long-term brand equity. AI pulls from everything, so years of brand building matter. Volvo’s long-term association with safety illustrates the strength of a settled meaning, for example.

A social post may feel fresh in isolation, but if it introduces a conflicting message, it adds confusion to the brand’s wider digital footprint.

That makes marketers’ impatience expensive. Your team may be tired of a campaign long before customers have properly registered it. Internal boredom is no reason to discard an association you are still building. Familiarity takes time to build and reinforce.

Pursuing new trends becomes a trap door. The brand needs to be clear about what must not change—ownable visual assets and core narrative—and what can change: executions.

Heinz shows the value of continuity. Years ago, there was discussion about removing its keystone logo because it seemed old-fashioned. The surrounding communications could be refreshed without discarding the symbol that made the brand recognizable.

Give agencies recognizable assets to work with and a clear meaning to reinforce. Find fresh expressions of the brand. Change the shirt, change the earrings, but remain recognizably yourself.

The same discipline applies to promises. Make sure your claims reflect what your business actually does, and provide evidence to support them.

The strongest brands give people reasons to remember them and machines clear signals to work with. Build those together, consistently over time, and you give both audiences a reason to choose you.

#10224. Why New York City’s grocery store plan is not just about food

New York City is moving closer to launching its effort to counter food inflation by opening five city-run grocery stores. Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced in May 2026 that the first store would open in the Hunts Point neighborhood of the South Bronx in 2027, with another in East Harlem to follow.

Five stores, one in each borough, are unlikely to substantially change grocery prices in a city with nearly 1,000 supermarkets and more than 8 million inhabitants. But each could make a meaningful difference to the grocery bills of local shoppers by selling essentials at below-market prices.

Even with just five planned stores set to open in lower-income neighborhoods, the initiative has ignited fierce opposition from independent grocers, supermarket trade associations, and a coalition representing immigrant-owned food businesses.

What explains this pushback?

As a food policy scholar, I believe this opposition is about more than the immediate economic impact of five stores. It is about the precedent they could establish. Mamdani’s initiative challenges an entrenched expectation that the government should leave the provision of consumer goods to private enterprise even as it encourages businesses to invest in certain locations, regulates their activities, and helps low-income shoppers through various food assistance programs.

The reality is more complicated. For at least a century, New York’s food economy has not operated independently of government. In fact, public policies and investments have long shaped where supermarkets open, which businesses can operate with a profit, and how residents obtain food.

It’s just that they have done so in ways consumers often don’t see.

That is why the five grocery stores carry a broader significance, in my view. They offer a different model of public investment that makes the government much more visible in providing an essential service—and more accountable for its results. New Yorkers will get an opportunity to judge that contribution directly.

If the stores succeed, they may change not just what people expect to pay for groceries, but what they expect their city government to provide.

How the plan will work

New York City has committed $70 million to develop these stores, which will be open to all.

While they will be managed by private operators, the city will provide rent-free space, prioritize publicly owned sites, and ensure that essential foods are priced 30% below typical retail prices.

In this respect, the stores offer a “public option”—a government-provided good or service that exists alongside private alternatives, like public schools and city hospitals.

Municipal grocery stores would offer New Yorkers a similar choice alongside private retailers. But as a public option, they would create a visible alternative against which shoppers can judge privately owned stores, setting a benchmark for food prices and service quality. They would also demonstrate how public investment can be used to make an essential good more affordable.

At his May announcement, Mamdani described the proposed Bronx store and its surrounding development as “physical proof of our conviction that government can be a force for good.”

A fresh form of intervention

Government-supported food retailing has a long history in New York City despite opposition by existing businesses.

In 1934, Mayor Fiorello La Guardia’s administration began selling discounted milk to low-income families, but the initiative drew complaints from grocers about unfair competition. Independent merchants similarly protested the city’s efforts to subsidize a new Pathmark supermarket in East Harlem in the 1990s, warning that it would put local grocers out of business.

A more recent example is the city’s Food Retail Expansion to Support Health program, known as FRESH. Since 2009, it has offered supermarket developers and operators long-term tax breaks and zoning incentives to build or expand dozens of stores in underserved neighborhoods.

These incentives have helped increase grocery retail space, but shoppers don’t see the public support behind them.

FRESH is just one example of an approach toward supermarket financing that gained momentum in the 1990s, when governments sought to address social problems by encouraging private investment. Food insecurity was blamed on a scarcity of neighborhood supermarkets, not on prices being beyond reach for local shoppers.

Subsidizing new stores promised better nutrition and economic development without confronting poverty or inequality, and FRESH reflects that approach. Participating supermarkets must devote space to perishable foods, but they’re not required to offer affordable prices. That may be one reason why researchers have found that adding supermarkets to low-income neighborhoods, by itself, doesn’t substantially improve residents’ diets.

This hidden government role is hardly confined to grocery stores. Much of what government does for Americans is delivered indirectly, through tax credits, subsidies, and private institutions. Because the public contribution is obscured, people often give credit to private markets for the benefits provided by public policy, from student loans to healthcare.

This invisibility is a consequence of policy design and influences how citizens understand government, a phenomenon that political scientist Suzanne Mettler described as “the submerged state.”

Bringing the state into the open

Municipal grocery stores depart from the traditional model in two important ways.

First, they make affordability an explicit condition of public investment rather than the outcome of increased retail competition. Second, they make government’s contribution visible. For example, the stores will share distinct branding so shoppers know who’s responsible for the affordable food.

If the stores deliver reliable savings, shoppers may begin to see affordable food as something government can help provide, not an outcome determined entirely by private markets. When public benefits are obscured, people are more likely to underestimate government’s contribution to their lives. Visible programs, like a physical store in the neighborhood, make that contribution easier to notice and evaluate.

Visibility also creates accountability. A customer at a private supermarket that received a tax break to expand isn’t likely to tie the store’s prices or food quality to government policy. At a municipal grocery store, with clear branding, the connection is unmistakable.

To be sure, critics’ concerns deserve serious attention. Many independent grocery stores are owned by immigrant entrepreneurs operating on thin margins. Groups representing bodegas and independent supermarkets warn that a publicly subsidized competitor could draw away their customers. Some may lose business.

Yet East Harlem’s Pathmark demonstrates that new supermarkets and smaller retailers can coexist. Between 2000 and 2015, the number of small grocery stores and bodegas in the neighborhood increased from 100 to 126, while supermarkets rose from 10 to 18. That said, those figures don’t establish Pathmark’s effects on individual businesses.

The municipal stores’ impact on nearby retailers remains an open question. But the task for New York City is to ensure that private operators deliver excellent service and real savings, and that their commercial interests don’t undermine the public mission. It will also need to provide good working conditions and track effects on nearby businesses.

Ultimately, public ownership doesn’t guarantee success. But it makes the government’s responsibility for the outcome impossible to miss.

Nevin Cohen is a chair of the Department of Health Policy and Management at the CUNY Graduate School of Public Health and Public Policy.

#10223. Top 6 AI Text to Speech Tools in 2026: Features, Strengths and Limits

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Not long ago, a synthetic voice was easy to spot: flat, rushed and strangely stressed. Today, the best AI text to speech tools can read a script with natural pacing, switch accents, whisper or laugh on cue, and even speak in a voice cloned from a short recording. That makes them useful far beyond screen readers. Developers use them for product voice prompts, marketers for video voiceovers, teachers for course narration and writers for listening back to their own drafts.

This guide explains how modern text-to-speech works, what to look for when choosing a tool, and compares six options: OpenArt, ElevenLabs, Murf AI, Speechify, WellSaid Labs and Amazon Polly. Each section covers strengths, limits and the best use case. The details come from each vendor’s own pages at the time of writing, and plans, models and prices change often, so confirm current terms before you commit.

OpenArt’s AI text to speech tool lives inside a wider creative platform. You open the Audio tab, choose Create voice-over, select a model, paste your script, pick a voice, generate, listen and download. It runs in the browser with nothing to install. According to OpenArt’s page, you can switch between models for each script, including Fish Audio Drama 3, Eleven v4 and Eleven v4 Turbo.

The direction system is what makes it practical for storytelling. You add notes in square brackets, such as [whispering], [laughs] or [pause], directly in the script. OpenArt says Fish Audio Drama 3 gives close control over single words and mid-line changes of mood, while Eleven v4 reads the whole script to infer the emotion of each line and keeps the voice steady when you regenerate a line. Preset voices are labeled by accent, gender and age, and you can upload a recording of your own voice to clone it.

Because OpenArt also makes video and background music, you can build the voiceover, visuals and soundtrack in one place. It describes a Director mode for planning stories up to five minutes, and the voiceover can also be added in any video editor.

Pricing: New accounts get 40 free credits. Paid plans add monthly credits and watermark-free downloads, and commercial rights apply on eligible paid plans. Check the pricing page for current plans.

Best for: creators who want expressive voiceovers together with AI video and music.

ElevenLabs is one of the best-known names in AI voice. Its text to speech page describes a large voice library, voice design and both instant and professional voice cloning, with the latest model, Eleven v4, positioned as the most expressive. It also lists Eleven v3, Multilingual v2 and a low-latency Flash and Turbo family aimed at real-time use, and it claims support for more than 90 languages and accents, with the exact count varying by model.

For developers, there is a text to speech API with SDKs, which makes it practical for apps, games, agents and automated pipelines. The free plan includes 10,000 credits a month, and paid plans start with Starter at $6 a month, then Creator at $22 and Pro at $99, according to the vendor page, with introductory offers on the first month.

Pricing: Free plan with 10,000 credits a month. Paid plans from $6 a month as listed on the vendor page.

Best for: expressive narration, multilingual content and apps that need a voice API.

Murf AI positions itself as a studio for voiceovers. Its page lists more than 200 voices, built with permission and partnership from professional voice actors who earn royalties, and support for 35 or more languages for text to speech, with dubbing in 40 or more. The Studio editor offers pitch, speed and intonation controls and a custom pronunciation library, which helps with brand names and technical terms.

Murf also has an API. Its page describes Falcon 2 for conversational use with time-to-first-audio under 100 milliseconds, priced at $0.01 per minute, and Gen 2 for controllable voiceovers. Gen 2’s “Say it My Way” feature lets you record your own rendition so the model reflects your tone and inflections.

Pricing: Free plan with limits. Paid plan prices are on Murf’s pricing page.

Best for: marketing videos, training and presentations where you want to fine-tune delivery.

Speechify is built around reading aloud. You paste text or upload a PDF, DOCX, TXT or EPUB file, pick a voice, adjust playback speed and listen or download the audio. Its page lists more than 1,000 voices across 60 or more languages, including several regional English accents, and the tool works in the browser and in apps for iOS, Android, Mac and Windows, plus Chrome and Edge extensions.

The use cases lean toward productivity and accessibility: studying, going through emails and documents, language learning and support for people with visual impairments, dyslexia or ADHD. A free account saves your documents and syncs them across devices.

Pricing: You can start free. Paid plans are listed on Speechify’s pricing page.

Best for: students, professionals and anyone who wants to listen to documents and articles.

WellSaid Labs focuses on professional voiceover for businesses. Every voice is built from recordings of a real voice actor who consented and is paid when the voice is used, and the voices are licensed for commercial use. Its page describes hundreds of voices across languages, accents, tones and styles.

Pronunciation control is a highlight. You can highlight a word to see suggested pronunciations and save your choice to a team library that applies to every project, and set pacing, emphasis and pronunciation line by line. WellSaid also describes a Producer product that connects AI assistants to WellSaid through MCP and its API.

Pricing: Contact sales for a quote based on your voiceover volume.

Best for: corporate training, product marketing, courses and advertising where licensing and consistency matter.

Amazon Polly is Amazon Web Services’ text to speech service, and it is aimed squarely at developers. According to AWS, it supports more than 40 languages and language variants with over 100 male and female voices, and it works through APIs in your code. It supports SSML, the W3C standard markup for phrasing, emphasis and intonation, and custom lexicons that fix the pronunciation of acronyms and terms. Output formats include MP3 and OGG.

Pricing is usage-based. AWS lists a free tier for new accounts, with usage allowances that depend on the voice engine, so estimate your character volume before you decide. A short example shows how little code a basic request takes:

The sample uses the AWS SDK for JavaScript, calls the neural engine and sends SSML so that the pause and emphasis are explicit. Adjust the region, voice and engine to match what your account supports.

Pricing: Usage-based with a free tier for new accounts. See the AWS pricing page for current rates.

Best for: apps, IVR systems, notifications and any product that needs automated speech at scale.

Treat this table as a starting point. Features and limits change often, so test two or three tools with the same script.

Modern text-to-speech systems turn written words into audio through several stages.

Newer expressive systems go further by reading the whole script to infer emotion and context, and by accepting direction in the text itself, such as a bracketed note that says to whisper. That is why a single script can produce very different reads depending on the model and the instructions.

If you use a tool with SSML support, you can make a spoken code or number far clearer:

The say-as element tells the engine to read the number digit by digit, and the break and emphasis tags shape the rhythm. Supported tags and attributes differ between engines, so check the documentation for yours.

What is the best AI text to speech tool? It depends on the job. OpenArt suits voiceovers with video and music, ElevenLabs suits expressive multilingual audio, Murf AI suits studio-style control, Speechify suits listening, WellSaid Labs suits licensed corporate work and Amazon Polly suits developers.

Is AI text to speech free? Several tools offer free plans or credits, but limits are common. Examples include OpenArt’s free credits for new accounts, ElevenLabs’ free monthly credits and Murf’s limited free plan, which has no commercial licence.

Can I use AI voices commercially? Often yes on paid plans, but the rules differ by tool. Always check the current licence before publishing.

Can AI text to speech clone my voice? Some tools support it, including OpenArt and ElevenLabs, usually from a short recording of your own voice. Only clone voices you have permission to use.

What is SSML? Speech Synthesis Markup Language is a W3C standard that lets you control pauses, emphasis, pronunciation and pitch in synthetic speech. Amazon Polly is one service that supports it.

Which tool is best for developers? Amazon Polly and ElevenLabs both offer APIs, and Murf describes API options as well. Evaluate latency, languages, pricing and SDK support for your use case.

How do I make AI voices sound less robotic? Write conversationally, add pauses and emphasis, correct pronunciations and split long scripts into short sections. Choose a model that is designed for expressive reads.

AI text to speech is now good enough for real projects, but the right tool depends on what you are making. OpenArt is a strong first stop for expressive voiceovers alongside video and music, ElevenLabs offers a deep voice library and API, Murf AI and WellSaid Labs suit polished, controlled narration, Speechify turns documents into audio and Amazon Polly fits straight into developer workflows. Test two or three with your own script, check the licence and always listen to the full result before it goes live.

Around a decade after “Hey Google” made its debut, Google is introducing its first new always-listening hotword. “Hey Gemini” makes its debut on Google’s Intelligent Eyewear glasses powered by Android XR, with wearers able to use that hotword in place of “Hey Google.”

This is a move that doesn’t come as a huge surprise. If anything, it’s perhaps a bit overdue.

While the hotword you use really won’t matter much at the end of the day, “Hey Google” has been recognized by many to not roll of the tongue very nicely. It’s a phrase that’s easy to stumble over, where “Hey Gemini” is a bit smoother.

As for whether or not “Hey Gemini” will become the default on future product remains unclear, but it’s a change only available on glasses for now.

We’ve asked Google if both hotwords will be active on Android XR glasses, but it was implied that this is, in fact, the case. When paired to Samsung glasses, “Hey Bixby” may also be in play, as Samsung’s voice assistant is supported on Intelligent Eyewear. Exact functionality, though, is something we’re still waiting for more clarity on.
