A clever yet simple way to establish correlation.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The topic of U.S. trade controls precluding the export of Nvidia and AMD high-end AI accelerator chips to China has taken a few twists lately. Jensen Huang's affairs aside, it's an open secret in the industry that Nvidia's Blackwell silicon finds its way into China, whether physically or virtually. UnemploymentLabs, an independent research outfit, has come up with strong evidence that those chips were used for training open-weight Chinese AI models, including DeepSeek V4, Kimi K3.1, MiniMax-M3, and Ling-3.1-Flash.

The scientists are careful to hedge their findings, noting that while their math checks out, it does not reveal where the chips were, how they were accessed, or prove that export controls were broken. As far as we can tell, it's currently not illegal for Chinese companies to rent Blackwell hardware abroad, and even though Nvidia's grip is tightening, U.S. companies aren't strictly prohibited from doing so, as evidenced by the recent Tencent-Oracle deal.

This identification method is limited to models with open weights, and depends on both hardware and software stacks used for model training — and yet it's both clever and simple, like the Egg of Columbus.

Let's establish some base facts. First, different AI accelerator families have unique counts of shader modules (SMs), marginally analogous to CPU cores — Nvidia's Hopper chips have 132, Blackwell B series have 148, and Blackwell GBs come with 152. Second, while there's more than one software stack for training AI models, PyTorch and its CUDA-aware friends are by far the most widely used on the green team's hardware.

The first step for training a model is initializing its weights, or how strongly the model considers each individual input. In modern LLM architectures, their initialization goes through a randomization step in which their values are adjusted plus/minus pseudo-randomly, using cuRAND — as in, randomly, but a seed starting value results in the same adjustment figures every time.

As you'd expect, doing this for an entire model is a lot of computational work, so this process is spread out across all the SMs, further subdivided into threads. For large weight sets, the thread count per SM is 2,048 for Blackwell and Hopper silicon, and it's surely carefully chosen and optimized for.

The researchers repeated a facsimile of the initialization process using the same chips, software, and thread counts. Using relatively simple statistical analysis, they spotted that their final statistical distribution of weight values precisely matched that of DeepSeek, Kimi, et al. As a test, they changed the SM and thread counts, and predictably, the correlation completely broke down.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

This let them pick out each family of Blackwell/Hopper chip used for each model, and eventually they also figured out an approximate count of cards used. They cannot, however, pinpoint which exact variation produced the weights, as this analysis is linked to initialization layout counts alone, thus SM count and usage pattern — not to VRAM capacity, memory bandwidth, or other characteristics that distinguish individual cards.

What about AMD cards like the MI300X, or other silicon with a high enough SM count, using the same software stack? The scientists say that it's not impossible that an AMD card could be set up to show up as two groups of 152 or 148 shaders, although we imagine there'd be little reason to do so. Nevertheless, for DeepSeek V4, they also ruled out that possibility by analyzing the actual weight values themselves, and found that AMD cards still didn't produce the same weight value pattern.

#10220. The chip war never ended

It’s no secret that the world runs on computer chips. 

This became clear during the pandemic, when a race for even basic chips needed to operate cars and other devices set back manufacturing timelines across the world. Beltway policymakers are reminded of just how important semiconductors are to the world every time China seems to move toward invading Taiwan, which raises the specter that the country could subsume control of TSCM, the most prominent computer chip contract manufacturer. 

Now Jensen Huang’s exit from Nvidia, which comes after reports of at least three known extramarital affairs—one of them with an alleged spy for the Chinese government—has thrown the world’s supply of computer chips back in the spotlight. With stocks falling and no obvious succession plan, it’s not clear what the future of Nvidia is right now, or how it might jostle the broader semiconductor ecosystem. 

“Many companies that have in the past relied on Nvidia will be watching very carefully to see whether they can rely on Nvidia going forward, and if not, they might turn to competitors,” says Chris Miller, a Tufts University professor and author of the 2022 book Chip War, which documents how the world came to depend on these tiny components.

Fast Company chatted with Miller on November 12 about Washington, D.C.’s response to the Huang scandal, Nvidia’s future, and the prospect of keeping advanced semiconductors out of countries like China. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. 

You’ve followed the chip industry for quite a long time. Are you surprised by what’s happened over the last few weeks? 

Jensen was an extraordinary CEO for 33 years, since Nvidia’s founding. [He] deserves a lot of the credit for the company’s extraordinary rise, but also deserves a lot of the blame for a series of poor decisions that have led not just to his ouster, but to a period of crisis for the company. Jensen really was central to Nvidia’s success, and he ran the company in a pretty unique way. He had 60 different people reporting to him directly, so there wasn’t a sort of standard corporate hierarchy, which worked really well for a long time. 

But it means that now that he’s gone, it’s not obvious who can fill his shoes. There’s not really a deputy who was waiting in the wings to take over. 

I’m curious about the history of espionage attempts like what’s being alleged here. 

There is some history during the Cold War, for example. There were efforts by spies from the Soviet Union or Eastern European countries to get access to sensitive technology by getting close to semiconductor executives. But I think the scale of this is kind of unique. First, that it happened to such a central company in the U.S. tech ecosystem, the most valuable company in the world. That’s somewhat unique. 

The second thing that’s unique is that the affair in question was both with a major customer, which shouldn’t have happened, as well as an [alleged] Chinese intelligence asset. There were a series of failures of judgment for a person who was one of the most important people in the U.S. and really in the entire world’s technology sector, and that combination does make this case unique.

I’m wondering about unexpected winners or companies that stand to benefit from this happening, especially other companies in the GPU market.

There are going to be competitors of Nvidia that will see this as an opportunity to win market share. AMD, for example, produces GPUs like Nvidia. In addition, many of Nvidia’s key customers, firms like Amazon—which has a vast data center business—buy Nvidia GPUs, but also design their own chips that have comparable performance characteristics. 

Many companies that have in the past relied on Nvidia will be watching very carefully to see whether they can rely on Nvidia going forward, and if not, they might turn to competitors.

Some leaders on the left are arguing this scandal is made worse because there’s so much market concentration in the semiconductor sector, that we’re too dependent on a small set of companies. Does that ring true to you?  

The market’s concentrated right now, but it’s a market that is also highly competitive. It’s worth remembering the market for AI chips scarcely existed five years ago when ChatGPT was launched. . . . I think what we’re going to see over the next couple of months is that if Nvidia does face a prolonged period of distraction and chaos, competitors to Nvidia are going to win market share.

I would look at this as actually a quite competitive market with a bunch of different players that all have pretty advanced capabilities.

Is it feasible to wall off technology from China? I know Nvidia was even considering putting location tracking in some of its chips to keep them away from certain places, even if they’re sold on the gray or black market.

One of the ironies of this is that Nvidia, in general, and Jensen in particular, thought they could play a big role in dictating Washington’s technology policy and were naive to the fact that China was playing them by [allegedly] turning Jensen’s mistress into an intelligence agent. 

This is going to lead to a major reduction in Nvidia’s influence in Washington. Its influence in the White House is declining as well, and I think Washington will respond with tighter controls over where chips can be sent and which types of companies are allowed to buy large numbers of these chips when it comes to installing them in foreign countries.

#10218. AI is making software easier to build. Keeping it running is another story

These days, it almost feels like old news: Developers can now use AI tools to generate code, build features, and make changes in a fraction of the time they once needed. The problem now surfacing across businesses is that once software goes into production, teams still need to monitor, maintain, and fix it. A feature that takes minutes to build can introduce problems that take engineers hours to investigate.

Google’s 2025 DORA report, based on responses from nearly 5,000 technology professionals, found that greater AI adoption was associated with faster software delivery but reduced stability. While the researchers didn’t establish that AI-generated code directly caused more outages, their findings suggest that companies can produce software faster without necessarily becoming better at maintaining it.

That raises a critical question for companies investing heavily in AI coding tools: If development keeps getting faster, how much of the work involved in running software can also be automated? A growing group of companies is working to find out, developing AI systems that can investigate failures, identify possible causes, and, in some cases, take corrective action without waiting for an engineer.

MORE SOFTWARE, MORE TO MANAGE

Ishay Yaari, cofounder and CEO of DataAgent, a company developing autonomous remediation software, says the operational side of software development hasn’t advanced at the same pace as coding.

“More code, more frequent deployments, and more infrastructure changes naturally create more potential failure points,” he tells Fast Company.

For site reliability engineering (SRE) teams, that means managing applications and infrastructure that may be changing more frequently. When something fails, engineers must figure out what changed, identify the cause, and restore service.

Consider an application that begins crashing after an update. The cause could be faulty code, an incorrect configuration, insufficient computing resources, or a problem with another service. While monitoring tools may detect the failure immediately, engineers still need to examine logs, review recent changes, and investigate several possibilities before deciding what to fix.

Yaari says companies often respond to growing complexity by adding monitoring tools and collecting more data. That can help engineers see what’s happening, but it can also mean more alerts to investigate without necessarily improving how quickly problems are resolved.

The pressure isn’t necessarily coming from poor-quality AI-generated code. Even reliable code can be difficult to manage when applications, infrastructure, and dependencies are changing frequently.

In a recent analysis of AI-assisted development, Google’s DORA researchers found that developers saved time generating code but spent more time reviewing and verifying it. They also emphasized the importance of testing, feedback, and established engineering practices in turning faster development into better results.

For companies, that means the benefits of AI coding tools may depend partly on what happens after developers finish writing the code, particularly the ability of SRE teams to keep applications running reliably.

GIVING AI THE KEYS TO PRODUCTION

Software monitoring and observability tools have traditionally helped engineers detect problems and understand their causes. Now companies are trying to automate more of the response.

DataAgent is pursuing that approach. Its platform is designed to monitor applications and cloud infrastructure, identify potential issues, and help investigate them. Yaari wants AI to take on more of the operational work engineers currently perform manually.

Some failures have familiar remedies. An application might repeatedly crash because it doesn’t have enough memory. A deployment might fail because of an incorrect configuration. Or a new release might introduce errors that disappear when the system returns to an earlier version.

Companies already use automation to address certain problems through predefined rules. AI could extend that capability by examining the circumstances, identifying likely causes, and selecting an appropriate response.

Yaari says DataAgent’s platform is designed to understand both the infrastructure supporting an application and the application itself, including how services interact, what the application is expected to do, and how its behavior changes after an update.

The aim is to recognize problems that don’t fit a predefined rule. But identifying a likely solution is one thing. Allowing software to make changes to a live application is another.

Consider a deployment that introduces errors. Rolling back to the previous version may restore service, but if the update also changed a database or introduced new dependencies, reversing it could create additional problems. That’s why the ability to act matters as much as the ability to diagnose.

HOW MUCH SHOULD AI BE ALLOWED TO FIX?

In its 2026 State of AI-First Operations report, PagerDuty found that 44% of surveyed organizations required human involvement when AI was used to fix problems affecting customer-facing systems, while 43% required it when coordinating incident responses across teams.

Even companies adopting AI for operational work appear reluctant to give it unrestricted authority over critical systems.

Yaari agrees that some decisions should remain with people. He points to actions such as deleting large amounts of data, disabling security controls, or exposing sensitive information as examples that should require approval.

“The goal is not to remove humans from SRE; it is to remove humans from the repetitive operational work that machines can handle safely,” he says.

Companies must determine which systems an AI agent can access, what changes it can make, and when it must request approval. They also need records of what the agent did, particularly when an attempted fix fails.

Another consideration is the cost of monitoring and observability software. Applications generate vast amounts of logs, performance measurements, and other operational data. Companies pay to collect, store, and analyze that information, often across several platforms. Adding AI can create further expenses if it requires transferring large amounts of data to external services.

Yaari argues that more analysis should happen closer to where applications run. DataAgent is pursuing a distributed approach, with agents deployed within customers’ infrastructure to reduce the amount of data sent elsewhere.

Its published documentation describes local monitoring alongside cloud-based AI analysis and guided incident investigation. Yaari’s responses describe broader autonomous remediation capabilities. The company has not provided independent performance data establishing how much operational work or cost those capabilities can eliminate.

WHAT HAPPENS TO THE ENGINEER?

Yaari expects engineers to spend less time investigating repetitive incidents and more time designing systems, setting operational policies, and deciding what automated tools should be allowed to do.

“The fundamental shift is from people operating infrastructure to people managing autonomous infrastructure,” he says.

That could allow smaller engineering teams to support more applications, but it would also require them to understand how automated systems make decisions—and what happens when those decisions are wrong.

Engineering skills may evolve as a result. System architecture, security, reliability, and the ability to investigate unusual failures could become more important as routine operational work becomes easier to automate.

Google’s DORA research found that organizations with strong engineering practices were better positioned to benefit from AI-assisted development. The same lesson may apply to AI-powered operations. Companies will still need reliable processes for testing changes, responding to incidents, and evaluating whether automated fixes work.

The software industry has made considerable progress in helping developers produce code faster. Now it’s trying to bring some of that speed to keeping applications running.

If AI eventually handles both, engineers may spend less time performing individual tasks and more time deciding what the systems they build should do, how they should behave, and when a person needs to intervene.

#10215. Thinking of quitting your job? Don’t until you consider this factor

You know that stinging sensation you get when your coworker gets the promotion that you thought was yours? Or that sinking feeling of doom when you realize that a new hire could take over your role? Most likely, that voice within will tell you: “You’re falling behind.”

You are, however, likely ignoring an important emotional experience happening at the same time. It’s envy: simply wanting something that someone else has. Because of the stigma and shame attached to this “deadly sin,” we tend to want to suppress envy without even knowing it. It’s understandable, but also a huge inadvertent mistake.

If you’re a conscientious high achiever, or someone smart and caring, it is easy to see someone else’s success and start questioning your situation. Envy is a universal emotion. It is also normal to wonder if it’s time to make a big change, like looking for a new job or even a new career. But examining your envy first can help you avoid costly career pitfalls.

Beware of ‘Premature Game Switching’

A common reaction to workplace envy that I see among my coaching clients is to make a change. This feels like being proactive, but it is giving up on the current situation too soon, or what I call “premature game switching.” You see someone getting ahead or getting what you want in the game you’re playing. You jump the gun and assess that you can’t obtain what you want or win at this game, so you opt out and choose a different contest.

Doing something feels better than doing nothing. When we avoid taking a beat to study our envy, however, we ignore critical data.

All negative emotions have what is called “signaling value,” demanding that we pay attention to what is important. Fear helps us see danger. Grief occurs when we lose someone dear. Envy helps us see what we truly desire and avoid “desire confusion.”

Thanks to savvy advertisers and social media, we are inundated with opportunities to feel what the philosopher and critic René Girard called “mimetic desire.” We tend to want things that those around us want. While “keeping up with the Joneses” used to include only neighbors or people we encounter in real life, the blast radius for envy has widened. Now we can see many more things that many more people have. We don’t often see how these cloud our judgment.

Envy gives us a chance to see what we really want.

Heed the SIReN

To examine envy, start by looking at its four key components, or “SIReN.”

First, S is “similar target.” According to the social psychologist Abraham Tesser’s Self-Evaluation Maintenance model, we tend to compare ourselves to those who are just ahead of us, our peers or our coworkers. We envy them, while we admire those far beyond us. This provides hope, telling us that we’re not as behind as we think we are. You feel envious of the promotion, for example, because it was within your reach.

Second, I is “intangible desire.” What we truly want is not the thing itself but the feelings we believe we will experience once we have it. It isn’t really the promotion, but what it represents to you, which could be a variety of things: financial security, recognition as an expert, or the opportunity to mentor others.

Third, Re stands for “relevant comparison.” We envy in domains or areas that are important to us. If we care about our careers, we’re likely to experience career envy. It pinpoints more specifically what matters to us and where we may want to focus more energy. I, for example, don’t envy people who have podcasts, but I do envy other nonfiction authors.

Finally, N is “negative emotion.” The unpleasant feeling is a gauge. If we’re able to close the app and forget about what we saw, the envy was fleeting and perhaps not worth dwelling on. If it lingers long after you put down your smartphone, you may want to take another look at why you’re feeling that way.

Next, Channel Envy in the Right Direction

Social scientists, including Jens Lange and Jan Crusius, have shown there are two kinds of envy: benign and malicious. Malicious envy tends to occur when you’re preoccupied with the person who has what you want, while benign envy is when you focus on what it is that you want. The Right Reverend Allen Shin, Bishop Suffragan of the Episcopal Diocese of New York, recently said that with malicious envy you cede your agency to the person you envy. But when you try to figure out how to get what you want, you keep your agency.

After examining your envy and figuring out the intangible desire, the next step is to figure out some “skill-building microactions.” Ask yourself: “What tiny activities should I test out to see if I can get closer to what I want?” If, for example, you realize that the intangible desire from wanting a promotion is financial security, then quitting your job will likely become a costly error. Instead, boosting your personal finance acumen might be a better option. Or, if you’re realizing that a promotion to you means mentoring others, then perhaps learning how to get reengaged with your alumni association and finding ways to mentor younger alumni might be a way to get more immediate satisfaction.

Finally, when we can direct our envy toward meaningful work, deepening relationships and serving others, we can feel more satisfied with our lives and do some good.

Malaysia plans to introduce a new law requiring data center operators to disclose their AI accelerator imports and power consumption to prevent diversion of restricted hardware to countries like China and optimize the use of the country’s power infrastructure, reports Malay Mail. The authorities also plan to charge data center operators for unused electricity capacity they reserve. While the idea to use power consumption to detect potential GPU smuggling has merit, it also has flaws.

Malaysia's Minister of Investment, Trade and Industry Datuk Seri Johari Abdul Ghani acknowledged on Thursday that some companies had rented space in Malaysian data centers to import GPUs legally, which they then shipped abroad in smuggling operations. To prevent such practices, Malaysia's Digital Ministry is now reviewing existing legislation to determine whether local authorities can take action against entities that re-export processors subject to U.S. export bans. The minister stressed that Malaysia wants AI accelerators imported into the country to be used domestically.

The proposed legislation will require data center operators to disclose the number of GPUs they import, their power consumption (presumably nameplate power consumption), the physical locations of their facilities, and the identities of operators and hyperscale customers. The government intends to track data center operations throughout their lifetime rather than limit oversight to the project approval stage.

Meanwhile, data center operators will have to pay for all the electricity capacity they reserve, irrespective of their actual power consumption. For example, if a data center secures 100 MW of power capacity but only uses 50 MW, its operator will still have to pay for the remaining 50 MW. The measure is meant to discourage companies from reserving electricity capacity they may not need for another one to three years. As an added bonus, the measure will further discourage rerouting AI hardware to China while pretending it is used in Malaysia.

While data on power consumption could help Malaysian authorities spot suspicious discrepancies between AI GPU imports and actual data center operations, it is virtually impossible to accurately determine the number of AI accelerators deployed at a facility based on power consumption alone. For example, Nvidia's H100 and H200 SXM GPUs are rated at 700W, whereas its B200 SXM accelerators are rated at 1,000W, yet neither necessarily consumes its rated power under actual workloads.

Furthermore, without knowledge of server configurations, the power consumption of CPUs, memory, storage, and networking equipment, or the power usage effectiveness (PUE) of a particular facility, any estimates of the number of operational GPUs would be imprecise, to put it mildly. Also, there may be a considerable delay between GPU imports and their actual deployment. As a result, reliable verification would require physical inventory audits or other mechanisms to track individual processors.

Johari said that Malaysian authorities were prepared to cooperate with their U.S. counterparts and provide information about facilities that house particular GPUs upon request. However, the minister did not specify whether the new legislation would require data center operators to disclose GPU models and serial numbers, or whether authorities would conduct on-site inspections.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Malaysia has emerged as a major destination for data center investments in Southeast Asia as cloud service providers and AI infrastructure companies expand their presence in the region. To date, Malaysian authorities have approved 117 data center projects, 55 of which are already operational, according to Johari. The proliferation of local AI data centers makes Malaysia a suitable venue for rerouting restricted hardware to countries like China, as it is easier to hide a needle in a pile of needles than in a haystack.

#10209. Data-Driven Pages That Never Go Stale: A Practical Guide

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Every developer has shipped the other kind of page: a lovingly written article or landing page that peaks on launch day and then quietly rots. Screenshots age, statistics expire, rankings slide. Data-driven pages play the opposite game. Built from a living dataset, they republish themselves daily, grow to thousands of URLs, and answer questions nobody had asked when the site launched. This guide breaks down how they work, using a real fan-run stats site as the running example: one public dataset in, more than ten thousand fresh pages out.

Static pages lose ground because the web moves and they do not. Facts expire, competitors publish fresher answers, and search engines reward pages whose information matches today. A page that cannot update itself must be rewritten by hand, so most sites update a few pages and abandon the rest.

Freshness is not one rule for the whole web; it depends on the query. Nobody needs a CSS tutorial rewritten weekly, but statistics, prices, availability and anything with a season attached decays on a schedule. Developers misjudge this constantly, treating every page like documentation when half their catalogue is really a perishable good. Serve a three-month-old stat as if it were current and readers learn the most damaging lesson a site can teach: do not trust the numbers here.

Then there is the maintenance maths. A hundred hand-written pages each needing one review a year is a hundred small debts, and the interest compounds as the catalogue grows. The team updates the flagship pages, promises to return for the rest, and quietly never does. Data-driven architecture is really a staffing decision disguised as a technical one: humans design the system once, and the system does the updating forever.

A data-driven site has three layers: a dataset that refreshes on a schedule, templates that turn records into pages, and URL patterns that map every meaningful combination users might search for. Change the data and every page changes; improve a template and ten thousand pages improve at once.

The running example makes this concrete. A fan-built Overwatch stats tracker republishes Blizzard's public hero data on a daily cycle. From that one feed it generates hero profiles, head-to-head matchup pages and multi-condition tier lists: 10,291 URLs in its sitemap, across six languages, with matchup pages alone accounting for 8,586 of them. Nobody wrote those pages. Somebody designed the system that writes them, which is a very different, and much more scalable, job.

The example runs on Next.js behind a CDN, but the stack is the least important layer of the three. The same pipeline feeding WordPress, Astro or a static site generator would look identical from the reader's side of the glass. Choose boring technology you already know, and spend your originality budget on the dataset and the templates, because that is where readers will feel the difference.

Generated pages stay useful when every URL must earn its existence with data. Set minimum thresholds before a page is published, give each template unique modules its siblings do not have, and noindex combinations with nothing to say. The line between a resource and spam is not automation; it is emptiness.

Quality gates work best when they are public and mechanical. The example site publishes its tier formula openly: 70% of the score from win rate, 30% from pick rate, and a hard floor that excludes heroes picked in under 0.5% of matches from topping the ranking, because a tiny sample cannot prove anything. That single floor is editorial policy expressed as code. Your version might be a minimum number of data points, a minimum price history, or a minimum review count — the number matters less than the fact that the gate exists and applies to every page equally.

Each template also needs modules its siblings cannot copy. A hero profile carries a seven-day trend and its best and worst matchups; a matchup page carries the head-to-head history; a tier list carries the movement since yesterday. Add a short human layer on top — a methodology page explaining the scoring, changelogs narrating what moved — and the catalogue stops reading as output and starts reading as a publication. Google's scaled-content rules target pages manufactured to manipulate rankings with little value; a page that answers a real query with real, current data is the opposite of that. The honest test for any generated URL is simple: if it vanished tonight, would a searcher lose an answer?

Start embarrassingly small: one dataset, one entity type, one template. A football club's results archive, a property portal's sold prices, your own product catalogue — anything structured and refreshed beats a grand plan. Prove one template earns traffic, then add combinations, languages and dashboards in that order.

What is programmatic SEO? Programmatic SEO means generating many pages from a structured dataset using templates, instead of writing each page by hand. Done well, each page answers a distinct search with real data. Done badly, it produces thousands of near-identical pages, which is where its reputation suffers.

Is programmatic SEO against Google's rules? No. Google's spam policies target scaled content created mainly to manipulate rankings, with little or no value for users. Pages generated from real data that answer real queries are publishing. The deciding question is whether a page helps its reader, not how it was produced.

How often should the data behind pages refresh? Match the refresh to how fast the underlying facts change. Sports and game statistics justify daily pulls, prices often need hourly checks, and reference data may only move monthly. Refreshing faster than reality changes wastes crawl budget and makes 'updated' stamps meaningless.

Do generated pages need unique written text? They need unique value, which is not the same thing. Identical paragraphs on ten thousand pages add nothing, but unique data, comparisons and trends are content in their own right. Add short human-written context per template, and let the data carry the differences between pages.

How many pages should a first project launch with? Launch with the smallest set that proves the template: one entity type, a few hundred pages at most. Validate that search engines index them and users engage before adding combinations and languages. Scaling an unproven template just manufactures tomorrow's cleanup job at industrial size.

The sites quietly winning the long game are not publishing more; they are publishing systems. One honest dataset, one well-built template and strict quality gates will outlast a hundred hand-written pages competing on freshness alone. Try it this week: take one dataset you already own, design a single template with four real modules, and ship fifty pages. Watch what the data does next.

Fast SSD leads to lower RAM requirements and smoother gameplay.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Gears of War: E-Day delivers an impressive visual and technical showcase. The game brings together several advanced graphics technologies, including Unreal Engine 5’s Nanite and Lumen, MegaLights, and RTX Mega Geometry for more accurate ray-traced shadows and reflections, alongside a range of upscaling and frame generation technologies.

However, today we’re focusing on a less-discussed technology that plays an equally important role in bringing this visually rich, densely detailed world to systems with more limited hardware resources: storage technology designed to reduce RAM usage.

We’ll begin by examining its behavior on a high-end system with plenty of resources to spare, before moving to a more modest configuration that better represents the hardware available to the average PC gamer. This will allow us to see how much of a difference the technology makes, particularly on lower-end systems.

In an interview with Digital Foundry, The Coalition explained how they leveraged the Xbox Series S’s fast SSD to bring the dense world of Gears of War: E-Day to a memory-limited system. By effectively using the NVMe SSD as an extension of system memory, they can dynamically load and offload complex city data in real time. This approach allows the game to stream the necessary assets for each scene just in time, overcoming the console’s limited RAM.

Digital Foundry notes that the true “special sauce” lies in The Coalition’s smart data management. The team employs advanced heuristics to determine which assets are fetched from the SSD and when, carefully balancing performance. Overusing this technique could harm frame rates, so the system is tuned to swap data only when it benefits the experience.

Gears of War: E-Day also supports DirectStorage, although based on our previous testing, this alone does not always result in high SSD activity or read rates.

YouTuber Mostly Positive Reviews shared his findings in a recent post on X, where he found higher-than-usual SSD activity in Task Manager when playing the game.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Gears of War E-Day is visually very impressive, but something has to be done with how the game either compiles shaders or streams data. My 14400F is constantly sitting at 80% CPU usage, 16GB RAM is maxed out, and disk read is sitting at a constant 120 MBps, with spikes up to 500 MBps. Will test this with the 9060 XT as well. These are settings I chose to maintain 60 fps, which it does, except for the massive shader compilation stutters every so often.October 7, 2026

Based on his findings, we decided to investigate further.

Task Manager does not use a low enough polling period to measure SSD activity accurately, so we used HWInfo with the polling period set to 20 milliseconds. We tested SSD activity across all of the game’s graphics presets at 4K using DLSS Quality.

In our previous tests of games that relied heavily on the SSD, none came close to sustaining 1 GB/s of average bandwidth. The highest we recorded was 366 MB/s in Forspoken at 4K with maximum settings, while many titles stayed well under 100 MB/s. Some games did show higher peak bandwidths, but these spikes lasted only a few milliseconds. For our purposes, it’s the sustained throughput – reflected in the average bandwidth – that truly matters.

In Gears of War: E-Day at higher settings, we essentially have a steady stream of a little over 1 GB/s at all times, indicating that the disk is indeed being utilized as an extension of system memory. As you can see, peaks hit up to 3.7 GB/s of throughput.

We measured RAM usage on our high-end system to see how much the game will use across each generation of SSD tested.

The game uses a significant amount of system memory, but having the game installed on an NVMe SSD – regardless of generation – saves about 2GB of RAM. The storage technology seems to be working as expected.

Since the game’s average read bandwidth far exceeds the limits of a SATA SSD, we expect that installing the game on one would lead to visual issues – and that is exactly what we observe.

In the first comparison, textures are slow to load, which noticeably reduces image quality. In the second comparison, lighting and shadows take some time to appear. While everything eventually loads correctly, running the game on a SATA SSD does hurt immersion.

We tested the game across four generations of SSDs to evaluate any impact on performance. Using a high-end system with ample memory, we aim to determine the behavior of the storage technology on a system that is not resource-constrained. We will then compare the performance of our laptop’s internal PCIe 4.0 NVMe SSD with that of a SATA SSD.

On a system with sufficient memory, installing the game on a SATA SSD has no measurable performance impact. The only drawback is the aforementioned visual degradation.

Now, we focused on our lower-end system with only 16GB of DDR5.

Now we start to see the benefit of installing the game on an NVMe SSD, especially on higher settings.

Although the average frame rate remains virtually identical on both the NVMe and SATA SSDs, increasing the graphics preset impacts the 1% lows. The NVMe SSD delivers smoother frametimes, resulting in a more responsive and fluid gaming experience.

While the concept isn’t entirely new – Windows already uses virtual memory to page data to disk when physical memory is exhausted – The Coalition has fine-tuned this technology specifically for their game. Their approach ensures that the data being paged out won’t noticeably slow down gameplay as it’s read from disk. In our testing, this technology successfully reduces RAM usage when the game is installed on an NVMe SSD.

Placing the game on an NVMe SSD also enables near-instant asset loading. For systems with 16GB of RAM or less, an NVMe SSD can deliver higher 1% lows, resulting in smoother performance. With RAM prices climbing and many players using machines with 16GB – or even 8GB – of memory, it’s reasonable to wonder if other developers will adopt similar techniques. For titles striving to create visually dense, richly detailed worlds, leveraging fast storage could be a practical way to preserve their vision on lower-end systems.

#10205. Nothing’s screen-less new gadget really looks like yet another AI recorder

Nothing has been teasing its first dedicated AI product and, as we expected, it really looks like an AI recorder.

Last week, Nothing CEO Carl Pei announced that the company would be launching its first “AI-native” product that doesn’t have a screen and “couldn’t have been an app.” Now, Pei is back with a brief teaser for the product, captioned “Context doesn’t live in a chat box.”

Nothing is keeping the details of what this product is a secret for now, but it’s becoming painfully obvious that this is an AI recorder.

The green and red lights paired with what looks like a record button paint a very clear picture. As we pointed out initially, Pei’s first post heavily implied this was some type of audio device. He said:

Meanwhile, the context that matters most never reaches the model at all. Think about the last time someone said something worth keeping: an idea over coffee, a throwaway comment that unblocks your whole week. What did you do? “Hold on, let me write that down.” Out comes the phone, and by the time you look up, the moment has moved on without you. Or you don’t bother, and it’s gone by the end of the day.

There are many AI recorders already on the market, admittedly with varying levels of quality, so we’ll have to wait and see how Nothing’s differentiates itself.

Yet, he is confident that Nvidia's board will conduct a thorough investigation.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Scott Bessent, U.S. Treasury Secretary, admitted that the U.S. export controls cannot prevent all the restricted hardware from reaching China or other adversaries, which is why the country allegedly obtained millions of restricted AI GPUs from Nvidia. At the same time, he questioned the efficiency of Nvidia's internal controls. called for accountability at Nvidia, criticized the company's general counsel, but stressed that it was unclear whether Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang knew about the potentially illicit practices.

"I think that there is a lot of leakage in the system, and we are constantly working to close that down," in an interview with CNBC (via @siliconmemes). "One thing here is that the story has been thus far on Jensen Huang's personal foibles. The real story here should be, did Nvidia know their client? And was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies? And I think it is important that anyone at the company there be held accountable for that."

Bessent admitted that despite strict U.S. export controls that prohibit sales of advanced AI GPUs to China, considerable quantities of restricted hardware may still make their way to the country. However, the Treasury Secretary does not believe that the U.S. needs to introduce more stringent export restrictions or grant government agencies additional powers to prevent GPU smuggling. Instead, the authorities should properly enforce existing regulations, according to Bessent.

Bessent also criticized Nvidia's general counsel Timothy Teter, who reportedly contacted the U.S. Department of Commerce to inquire whether U.S. authorities were behind the detention of Megaspeed's Alice Wong in Singapore. However, the Treasury Secretary declined to speculate about potential consequences for Nvidia if it turned out that some of its executives knew that their customers acted as intermediaries for Chinese entities. Meanwhile, Bessent expressed confidence that Nvidia's board of directors would conduct a thorough investigation into the matter.

"But let us just say, if this was happening, then there were not robust controls at the company," Bessent said. "We do not know for a fact that Jensen Huang knew this. The [general council] seems to have been very involved here, probably should have done more oversight rather than the haranguing [government officials at the U.S. DoC]."

Bessent also revealed that the Departments of the Treasury, War, and State, as well as the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative (USTR), had supported the addition of Megaspeed to the Entity List for months. However, the authority to impose such export restrictions belongs to the Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), which reportedly stalled efforts to blacklist Megaspeed for months as Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick feared that the move could worsen trade tensions with China.

#10202. Four excellent Garmin watches are on deep discount ahead of Black Friday

Garmin has a watch for every budget this year, and it’s clear the company is working on shipping more watches than ever at these prices.

After hunting for smartwatch deals over the past few weeks, it’s pretty clear Garmin isn’t playing around this year. I’ve found several older Garmin watches on sale this month, but now the company is extending the early Black Friday sales to some of its newest watches. Let’s start with those first.

The Garmin Forerunner 70 is the first budget-minded Forerunner watch in five years, and the white colorway is currently $50 off (20%), coming in at just $199, its lowest price ever. The Forerunner 70 is a fantastic-looking watch that packs the same Garmin OS as the more expensive models, including new Quick Workout features, 50 more workout modes, and an upgraded optical heart rate sensor and GPS modules over the previous budget Forerunner watch, the Forerunner 55.

The second new Garmin watch on sale today is the Venu 4 bundle, which is currently $105 off (19%), making it $454.99, this watch’s lowest price ever. The Silver/Gray colorway is the least expensive one. The slate model with a brown leather band is also $105 off, and while that model is normally the most expensive one anyway, this sale makes it $504.99. No matter which colorway you choose, the bundle includes:

The Venu 4 is the latest in Garmin’s most elegant line of smartwatches, packing a 1.4-inch circular AMOLED screen inside a stainless steel case. It tracks heart rate, Pulse Ox, HRV status, stress, women’s health (with skin temperature readings), advanced sleep with circadian alignment, and puts it all together in a Body Battery energy score so you can know what days to push harder (and which ones you really need to take it easy on).

If you’re OK with something just a little bit older, the Venu 3S and Fenix E are impressively solid choices at terrific prices:

I covered these deals a few days ago, and they’re somehow still around, which is impressive considering they’ve never been cheaper. The Fenix E features multi-GNSS navigation plus a 3-axis compass, gyroscope, barometric altimeter, pulse ox monitoring, respiration tracking, advanced sleep monitoring, real-time stamina tracking, and a training readiness score to tie it all together. All of this happens despite the watch lasting two weeks per charge.

And the Venu 3S is still loved by a ton of people in the Garmin community thanks to its gorgeous trim, lighter weight than the Venu 4, better battery life (by 1-2 days), and an OS some people prefer over Garmin’s newer designs. These watches are built to last you a long time, so feel good about investing in one, especially if you’re serious about staying healthy.

It's been a big week. Let's break it down.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Seismic appears to set the tone for this week's events in the hardware industry, and we've covered the biggest beats, including deeper dives on hardware and AI topics over on Tom's Hardware Premium. Stories this week are colored by the fact that Nvidia founder Jensen Huang has stepped away from his post as CEO. The ramifications are wide and far-reaching, as the company transformed from a gaming GPU manufacturer to an AI business over the past five years.

First up, it's not only hyperscalers and neoclouds that have their eyes on AI. An increasingly popular segment among enthusiasts is PCs dedicated to running local AI models. With so many choices on the market currently, from the recently released RTX Spark to AMD's Strix Halo platform, we take a look at two unlikely contenders that are now going head-to-head: Nvidia's DGX Spark and Apple's Mac Studio. We ran a suite of real-world and synthetic benchmarks across both devices and tested large models on both machines. With prices at eye-watering levels, it's more crucial than ever that you make the correct choice for your intended workloads.

DRAM capacity constraints have been an industry-wide sticking point as the AI buildout accelerates demand for dies. With costs spiraling across both client and enterprise hardware, AMD has shared further detail about MEXT, a predictive memory engine which aims to offer 99% of a server's performance while running on half the DRAM. Powered by a transformer model and clever use of flash storage, AMD is already running 145 servers with the system in place, with a view to expand that figure to 2,000 next year.

Next, we sat down with Cognichip's Chief Product Officer in an extensive interview to explore how the company is rolling out AI-powered chip design tools. Back in September, the company revealed a suite of proprietary AI models, named Artificial Chip Intelligence (ACI), which are specifically developed for semiconductor engineering. While the tools have yet to be used in a shipping product, it could substantially improve chip development productivity by automating labor-intensive tasks.

The Jensen Huang scandal deepens, as the now-former Nvidia CEO has become embroiled in a series of alleged extramarital affairs and has since resigned from Nvidia. While much of the past week's stories have centered on his relationship with alleged Chinese Spy Alice Huang, we explored the former CEO's unlikely relationship with Kang Wei, Ms. Huang's husband, who recently landed in hot water with China's Securities Regulatory Commission.

Nvidia-based compute remains difficult to find in China, especially as AI labs line up to order racks and newer cards like the RTX 5500 Pro, with over 6 million units reportedly ordered for the export-compliant GB202-based AI accelerator. But the Chinese AI labs that are chasing after Nvidia's tech may still have to pay a premium and ensure that they're running enough homegrown silicon to not fall afoul of Beijing's rules. We explore how some companies have now moved to renting compute in Southeast Asian countries like Malaysia and Singapore in an attempt to get around export controls.

Google's one of the biggest competitors to Nvidia, especially in the AI domain. The company's 8th-gen TPU lineup has now expanded even further, with two new chips designed for long-context agentic AI and security. These two new chips, TPU 8i Max and TPU 8tx, signal a further diversification across Google's eighth-generation TPU stack. While TPU 8i Max doubles the specs of the original TPU 8i, TPU 8tx makes a more interesting change to AMD's EPYC to serve its use in specialized security workloads.

Lastly, a new proposed framework aims to track how easy it might be for an AI model to break through its safeguards and generate potentially harmful content. The Frontier Model Foundation has proposed a Jailbreak Rating Framework which aims to classify the type and severity of a possible LLM jailbreak. With four scoring components in hand, the foundation aims to identify possible jailbreak vectors and inform labs of them before they happen in the real world, with potentially disastrous consequences.

#10199. Running WireGuard for a Development Team: The Hidden Cost of VPN Maintenance

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Setting up WireGuard on a small virtual server is a satisfying infrastructure task. Install the package, generate a key pair, open a UDP port, configure a peer, and connect a laptop. Within an afternoon, your staging environment can sit behind a private tunnel, and your internal dashboard can be restricted to traffic from a known address.

The initial setup is rarely the difficult part.

The real engineering work starts when the team changes. A developer joins, another leaves, someone replaces a laptop, a server needs patching, or a connection suddenly stops working. Each event creates a small maintenance task. Over time, those tasks become an operational responsibility that somebody must own.

This article examines what it takes to operate a self-hosted WireGuard VPN for a development team. We'll look at peer configuration, access management, troubleshooting, monitoring tools, and the engineering time involved. We'll also compare self-hosting with managed business VPN services so teams can make a decision based on their infrastructure needs.

WireGuard is a modern VPN protocol designed to establish encrypted connections between network peers. Its relatively small codebase, modern cryptography, and straightforward configuration make it attractive for developers who want control over their network infrastructure.

A basic WireGuard deployment typically involves:

A server with a reachable public IP address.

A private and public key pair for the server.

A UDP port through which peers communicate.

Peer configuration that defines which addresses are allowed through the tunnel.

A simplified server configuration might look like this:

The corresponding client configuration contains the client's private key and the server's public key:

These examples illustrate the basic relationship between a server and a client. A production configuration will also need appropriate firewall rules, routing, DNS settings, and a plan for distributing configuration securely.

The important distinction is that WireGuard establishes encrypted peer connections. It does not automatically provide a complete employee identity system, onboarding workflow, approval process, or audit dashboard.

Those responsibilities belong to the team operating the infrastructure.

Developers interested in using WireGuard on personal development devices can also explore SitePoint's guide to building a hardened mobile development environment with Termux, Docker, and WireGuard.

A peer is not just an entry in a configuration file. It represents a device that has permission to communicate through your network.

That makes peer management an access-control responsibility.

For a small development team, it is tempting to keep a single configuration file and update it manually whenever someone joins or leaves. This can work initially, but it becomes harder to manage as the number of devices increases.

A useful first step is to maintain a peer inventory:

The inventory should not contain private keys. Private keys must remain on their respective devices and should never be placed in a shared spreadsheet or source repository.

The inventory instead helps administrators answer practical questions:

Which device is associated with this tunnel address?

Has the peer been removed after the device was lost or replaced?

This information becomes especially important when a team uses the VPN to reach staging servers, internal dashboards, databases, or other development resources.

Manual onboarding is manageable when a team has only two or three developers. It becomes unreliable when several people join, leave, or change devices over the year.

A repeatable onboarding process should cover more than generating a key pair.

Confirm that the team member is authorized to access the environment.

Generate a key pair on the user's device.

Add the public key to the server's peer configuration.

Apply the appropriate routing and firewall permissions.

Deliver the client configuration through a secure channel.

Test access to the specific development resources the person needs.

Record the peer owner, device, and approval details.

Offboarding needs an equally clear process:

Identify every peer associated with the departing team member.

Remove the relevant public keys from the server.

Confirm that the configuration change has been applied.

Review any other credentials or allowlists that granted access.

An administrator can inspect the currently configured peers with:

The output helps identify peer public keys, transfer counters, and latest handshake information. It is useful for troubleshooting, but it should not be treated as a complete access audit or proof that a particular person is still authorized.

The broader lesson is to make access changes part of a documented workflow. A peer should not remain active simply because nobody remembers who created it.

One common network-design mistake is assuming that connecting to a VPN should give a developer access to every internal service.

A developer working on a frontend application may need access to a staging web server but not to the production database. A contractor may need access to one test environment without being able to reach internal administration tools.

WireGuard's peer configuration and the surrounding network controls should be designed around those requirements.

Separate tunnel address ranges for different groups.

Firewall rules that restrict traffic to approved services.

Cloud security groups that limit access to specific ports.

Application-level authentication for internal dashboards.

Separate production and staging network boundaries.

The exact implementation depends on the infrastructure. The key point is that VPN membership and application authorization are different controls.

A successful VPN handshake should not be treated as permission to access every resource behind the tunnel.

A VPN can appear simple when it works. Diagnosing it becomes more complicated when a developer is connecting from a home router, a hotel network, or a mobile hotspot.

Incorrect routing or AllowedIPs settings.

A server process or host becoming unavailable.

WireGuard provides useful inspection commands:

These commands help inspect peer information, check the service state, and review recent service logs. The exact systemd service name can differ depending on how the interface was configured.

Administrators should also monitor the underlying server. At minimum, that means checking:

Whether the WireGuard interface is active.

Whether disk or memory usage is approaching a limit.

Whether operating-system and package updates are pending.

A small virtual server may be inexpensive, but it is still infrastructure that needs an owner.

Teams working with alternative tunnel-based development workflows may find SitePoint's tutorial on setting up Cloudflare Tunnels with Docker Compose for persistent webhook debugging useful. It covers a different tunneling use case, but the operational questions around connectivity, service health, and troubleshooting are closely related.

A self-hosted VPN does not need to become a collection of manual tasks. A few established tools can make configuration, monitoring, and debugging more repeatable.

The core tool is, of course, WireGuard. Its command-line utilities allow administrators to inspect peers, manage interfaces, and review connection information. The official documentation is the best starting point for understanding configuration options and platform support.

Ansible can automate repeatable server administration tasks. A team could use playbooks to deploy configuration files, apply system updates, or standardize firewall settings across several VPN hosts.

Sensitive values should be handled with an appropriate secrets-management approach. Private keys should not be committed to a Git repository or stored in plaintext playbooks.

Prometheus is useful for collecting and querying metrics, while Node Exporter exposes Linux host metrics such as CPU, memory, disk, and network statistics.

These tools do not automatically provide a complete WireGuard security audit. They can, however, help identify resource problems and server-health issues before those problems become user-reported outages.

Uptime Kuma provides a self-hosted monitoring dashboard with notifications. It can help teams monitor the availability of a VPN host or related services.

A basic availability check does not prove that every VPN peer can connect successfully. For more meaningful monitoring, combine host checks with an end-to-end test from a separate network.

Wireshark and tcpdump help developers inspect network traffic when diagnosing connectivity problems.

For example, tcpdump can capture UDP traffic on the WireGuard port:

This can help determine whether packets are reaching the server. It does not decrypt WireGuard traffic or replace checks of routing, firewall rules, and peer configuration.

The right toolset depends on the size of the deployment. A team with one VPN server may only need WireGuard's own commands and basic host monitoring. A larger environment may benefit from automation, centralized metrics, and a documented incident process.

A self-hosted VPN can cost very little in direct infrastructure charges. However, the server invoice does not include the engineering time required to operate it.

Consider a hypothetical team with these assumptions:

Two people join and two leave during the year.

The team reviews or rotates device keys quarterly.

Patching and monitoring require about two hours per month.

Six troubleshooting incidents occur annually.

The estimated loaded engineering cost is $60 per hour.

The virtual server costs approximately $6 per month.

The following estimate illustrates how quickly maintenance time can exceed the infrastructure bill.

At $60 per hour, 46 hours represent approximately $2,760 in engineering time. The server adds around $72 per year, bringing the estimated total to $2,832.

These figures are illustrative, not a universal cost benchmark. A team with infrastructure automation and established monitoring may spend considerably less time. A team with frequent staff changes or strict audit requirements may spend more.

The useful exercise is to measure the work your own team performs. Track onboarding, access reviews, patching, incidents, and recovery time for a few months. That gives you a more realistic comparison than looking at hosting prices alone.

Self-hosting is not automatically the best option just because a team has developers who can configure servers.

A managed business VPN may be worth considering when the team needs centralized member management, simpler device administration, or a stable network exit address without maintaining the underlying VPN infrastructure.

Depending on the provider and plan, managed services may offer:

A central dashboard for adding and removing users.

Client applications for common operating systems.

Multi-factor authentication or identity integrations.

For example, PureVPN for Teams is one service in this category. Teams evaluating it—or any other provider—should check the current feature set, pricing, logging practices, access controls, and service terms before making a decision.

A managed service does not remove every security responsibility. The team still needs to decide who receives access, review permissions, protect user accounts, and understand how traffic and metadata are handled.

It also introduces vendor dependency and a recurring subscription cost. Those trade-offs should be considered alongside the engineering time saved.

There are situations where running WireGuard yourself is the more practical option.

You already operate infrastructure. If your team routinely patches servers, manages secrets, monitors services, and responds to incidents, maintaining a VPN may add relatively little work.

You need custom routing. A deployment that connects several private cloud networks, on-premises environments, or specialized subnets may require network controls that are easier to implement directly.

You have strict data-control requirements. Some organizations have policies that limit which third parties can handle network traffic or related metadata. Those requirements may favor infrastructure under the organization's own control.

You have a dedicated platform or security team. If someone is explicitly responsible for access management, monitoring, and incident response, self-hosting can fit naturally into existing operations.

You can automate the lifecycle. Infrastructure-as-code, configuration management, documented peer inventories, and tested recovery procedures can reduce repetitive work and make a self-hosted deployment easier to maintain.

The important distinction is between a deliberately operated service and a one-off server that nobody owns.

Before choosing an approach, ask the following questions:

Who is responsible for the VPN six or twelve months after deployment?

How many people and devices are likely to join or leave?

How are public keys and peer configurations tracked?

How quickly can access be revoked when a device is lost?

Which internal services should each developer be able to reach?

Do you need a fixed egress IP for external allowlists?

What monitoring and recovery process exists if the server fails?

Do your customers or internal policies require access logs or formal reviews?

Does your team have the time and expertise to maintain the infrastructure?

Would a managed service cost less than the engineering time and operational risk it replaces?

If your team already has mature infrastructure practices and needs custom network control, self-hosting may be a sensible choice.

If the team is small, access changes frequently, and nobody has time to own another server, a managed service may be more practical.

WireGuard is an excellent protocol, and deploying it can be a straightforward engineering task. But operating a VPN for a development team involves more than establishing an encrypted connection.

Peer management, onboarding, offboarding, network permissions, monitoring, patching, and troubleshooting all require ongoing attention.

The right choice depends on the team's infrastructure experience, security requirements, size, and available engineering time. Self-hosting offers control and flexibility; a managed service can reduce operational work. Neither option removes the need for sound access-control practices.

Before deciding, calculate the maintenance effort, identify who will own the service, and make sure the design can be maintained as the team changes.

The cost example uses illustrative assumptions rather than current vendor pricing. Managed VPN features and prices can change, so verify provider details before purchasing.

Getting your hands on fast NVMe storage for your PC or laptop has become extremely challenging. That said, the Samsung 990 SSD is currently available at a discounted price of $189.99, against its original list price of $229.99 on Amazon. Although the $40 saving might not seem that impressive, deals on high-performance internal SSDs are becoming harder to come by amid the ongoing NAND and DRAM crisis. If you've been holding off on a storage upgrade, this could be a good opportunity to pick up a reliable, high-speed SSD.

The Samsung 990 is a PCIe 4.0 NVMe SSD that uses Samsung's latest V9 QLC NAND flash memory and a DRAM-less controller. It was introduced earlier this year with MSRPs of $269.99 for the 1TB model and $529.99 for the 2TB model. The 1TB model offers sequential read and write speeds of up to 7,150 MB/s and 6,450 MB/s, making it an excellent option for everyday computing, gaming, and handling large files. Samsung rates the drive for up to 400TB of written data, although it offers just three years of warranty. It features a single-sided M.2 2280 design, which should make it compatible with a wide range of desktop motherboards, laptops, and even mini-PCs.

Samsung's 990 is rated for read speeds of up to 7,150 MB/s and write speeds of up to 6,450 MB/s, offering plenty of bandwidth for modern games, large files, and everyday applications.

In our testing of the 2TB variant, we found that the Samsung 990 delivers reasonably good all-around performance, particularly for gaming and everyday applications. It offered similar performance to the Samsung 990 EVO Plus in some tests. However, it fell behind competing drives such as the Crucial P310 and WD Blue SN5100 in others, particularly during file transfers. One of its biggest advantages is its large write cache, which allows it to maintain speeds of nearly 6,100 MB/s for more than 57 seconds before performance drops once the cache is exhausted. Its power efficiency may not be the best, but overall it is a competent budget PCIe 4.0 SSD.

For anyone upgrading from an older SATA SSD or a traditional hard drive, the Samsung 990 should offer a noticeable improvement in boot times, application loading, and overall system responsiveness. At its current price of $189.99, it is also a suitable option for expanding game storage without spending a fortune.
